Northern railway was compelled to make an arrangement for exchange of traffic with the Intercolonial railway whenever the Government should demand it. Chapter 6 of the Statutes of 1911, subsection (b) of section 14, reads:
On the request of the Government, to make arrangements with the Intercolonial railway for the interchange of traffic between the company and the Intercolonial railway at Montreal, for such period as the Governor in Council determines, and upon such terms as are agreed upon between the parties, and if the parties fail to agree, the terms shall he fixed by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
After a great deal of discussion with the owners of the Canadian Northern railway, this clause was inserted compelling the Canadian Northern railway, whenever the Government should demand it, to make a traffic arrangement with the Intercolonial railway subject to the Board of Railway Commissioners if the Government and the company could not agree.
At Montreal.

Which would make it absolutely necessary to have an interchange of traffic all along the line, because you could not very well have two or three exchanges. The reason why the. statute did not provide that the Canadian Northern railway should immediately give an interchange of traffic was that there was not much traffic to interchange at that time, as the Canadian Northern railway was not completed. In the second place, there is a contract at the present time for the interchange of traffic between the Intercolonial railway and the Grand Trunk railway, which it would not be easy to break, and perhaps not desirable. The Government of that day did that, and I think the present Government will agree that the Grand Trunk railway, itself, when the Grand Trunk Pacific railway is finished, will probably want to make some arrangement to have its freight carried from Montreal to Quebec, and the eastern ports, over the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. An arrangement was made that when the Government should express a desire for a contract, the Canadian Northern railway would be compelled to exchange traffic with the Intercolonial railway. I am not finding fault with the arrangement in this respect at all, but some hon. gentlemen have expressed the view that that was forgotten in 1911. Nothing of importance was forgotten in 1911, as I will try to show my hon. friend. My hon. friend referred to another point, and that is the shipment of goods to Canadian ports. I do not agree here with the

Prime Minister, who rather thought that leaving out the words ' unless otherwise routed ' makes it compulsory for the Canadian Northern railway to carry the traffic to Canadian ports. That is an omission of words that makes no difference in actual practice. If I ship a bushel of grain from the West, I am the owner of that grain and I say how it is to go. I select the route. If I desire to ship it by one particular route the Canadian Northern railway cannot take my grain by any other route. They have to carry it to the designated port by the route I choose. That is what the statute of 1911 says. Every business man in the House will agree with me that a shipper has perfect control over the routeing of his goods. If I order some goods from John Brown, and send them by the Canadian Northern railway to Winnipeg, and then on by the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, do you think I am not the controller of those goods ? The Canadian Northern railway must hand them over to the party whom I designate. So that leaving out the words ' unless otherwise routed ' makes it read a little more smoothly but does not alter the meaning at all. Let me read the statute of 1911, and lest a wrong impression should go abroad, I want to point out that there is nothing in this that was not in the statute of 1911 when the bonds were guaranteed on the line from Port Arthur to Montreal. The statute reads:
It is hereby declared that the aid herein provided for is granted by the Government for the express purpose of encouraging the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. Before such aid is granted the Governor in Council shall require the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company to enter into an agreement undertaking that all freight originating on the line of the Canadian Northern Railway Company or its branches, or on the line of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined to points in Canada be carried over the Canadian Northern railway or the Canadian Northern Ontario railway, or the connections of either of them, or over any railway within Canadian territory; and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports; and that the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company shall not in any matter within their powers directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall, in all respects, in good faith, use their utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely, the development

of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.
Those conditions were imposed when aid was granted to the Canadian Northern in 1911, and although the wording is not exactly the same in this case, the meaning is identically the same. No railway or transportation company can take goods of mine contrary to my directions, and they are liable to a penalty if they do so. If goods be shipped without being specifically routed, it is the duty of the Canadian Northern railway, and has been ever since 1911, to take them to Canadian ports. It is the same in 1914 as it was in 1911. If the shipper routes his goods one way the Canadian Northern railway, as the carrying company, has no power to carry them by a different route. I think it was the Solicitor General who ridiculed this 1911 arrangement, saying that if we had taken the road over we would have had no terminals and consequently could not operate. I think that was the trend of his argument. I am afraid my hon friend has not read the statute. Even that wa3 provided for, and I think when Mr. Lash was working this out he had this in his mind before he discussed it with the Solicitor General. The terminals were specifically provided for in the statute of 1911. The terminal companies were separate companies, and I say to my hon. friend and to the House that with the indebtedness against the terminal companies I did not think the second or third mortgage on them would have been any security at all. Let me read what provision we made in 1911 in case the road should come under that mortgage. Subsection c of section 14, chapter 6 of the statutes of 1911, provides:
That in the event of default, and of the consequent acquisition by the Government, or by any railway company other than the company, of the line hereby aided, neither the company nor the Canadian Northern Railway Company will oppose any application to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada for an order providing for the use by the Government, or by such other railway company, of terminals at Port Arthur, Ottawa, and Montreal, or either or any of them, owned or controlled by the company or by the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
So that it was provided that if the line defaulted and became the property of the Government the Canadian Northern would not oppose any application to the Board of Bailway Commissioners to let either the Government or the new owner of the railway use their terminals at Montreal, Ottawa, and Port Arthur. My hon. friend says that 2401
is not as good as we have it. Why? The terminal companies are separate companies and the road now has to make arrangements with separate companies if they want to use the terminals no matter whether the stock is controlled by the same people or not. They are a separate entity and they have to make their arrangements as to what it will cost the Canadian Northern, or the Canadian Northern Ontario, to use these terminals. In the statutes of 1911 we were placing the Government, if it came into possession of the railway, in exactly the same position as the railway itself in regard to the use of these terminals.
Let me turn to some of the securities of 1911. My hon. friend rather drew a distinction between the bargain of 1911 and the proposed bargain of this year as outlined in the resolutions. Perhaps I may be blunt in my expression but I would say that there is no use of beclouding the *situation with words, words, words and pages, pages, pages. The securities outlined in this resolution, to my mind, are nothing but words and sentences and do not form any real security. I would rather have a first mortgage on 500 miles of the Canadian Northern railway than all the securities that my hon. friend has gathered together in this resolution. In 1908 the Government of the day got a first mortgage on the line then aided. In the succeeding year it got, in addition to a blanket mortgage on other lines, a first mortgage on the line aided. In 1911 it did not take mortgages On stock, except in two small instances, 'it did not take stock that had no value, but it did take a first mortgage on the line aided and that first mortgage is worth more than the value of the full amount of this guarantee by the Government in 1911. The line from Ottawa to Port Arthur, when it is completed, will be the best part of the Canadian Northern system up to date and it will take many thousands, yes, many millions, of dollars, to bring other parts of the system up to the standard of the road between Ottawa and Port Arthur, if it is built up to the standard. When that guarantee was given there were conditions as to the standard of the road comprised in the guarantee. In the first place, heterodox as it may seem on the other side of the House, we stipulated that they must build steel and concrete bridges and that for the smaller streams they could for the time being use wooden trestles but that the Governor in Council would see that they were replaced by steel structures as soon as possible. The 1 soon as possible '

has come now and we are asked to supply the money to make all these improvements and to bring the road up to standard. I am not pointing out these things about the policy in 1911 in any fractious way but I want to make it clear from the standpoint of the late Government, and from my own standpoint, as I was directly responsible, that in a first mortgage on the line from Ottawa to Port Arthur we had a far better security than is Proposed now in this list of securities that has been placed before the House. In fact, there is no first mortgage on any real estate in these resolutions except a first mortgage on the 4 p.m. Brocltville and Westport railway, running 45 miles from Brockville north with a 56-pound rail.
Ever since I entered this House we have been discussing the question of branch lines. I have taken the ground, sometimes disagreeing with members of the House and, I think, possibly disagreeing with some of my own friends, that it is the duty of the Government, in connection with a Government-owned road, not only to provide branch lines where they will pay, but to provide branch lines where the people have been in the country for years and require the transportation because that is the only way more people can be brought into the country. I have taken that ground. But now in this discussion one of the reasons .given why these roads were not amalgamated is that some branch lines which do not pay might be cut off. That is a retrograde policy. I think the Government's duty, in dealing with this great enterprise and in announcing their policy was to declare that they would take over these branch lines whether they were paying propositions or not if the necessities of the people-settled in the districts served by the lines required it. Instead of that they gave, as a reason why these roads should not be amalgamated, that if the time came to take them over, they would be in a position to cut off the lines which were not paying a profit. That announcement will not be encouraging to the settler in the East or the West and I think the Government will have to revise that policy when the Bill comes up for discussion and will have to admit that that is not the reason for the non-amalgamation, as I think it is not.
What are the reasons?
My hon. friend wants to know what are the reasons?
I think my hon. friend *could give very good reasons himself.

province of Ontario a law under which the assessor asks us to make certain affidavits and statements as to our income, and there is not much opportunity of getting around that. We could do something similar in this case, without prying into matters that perhaps might be considered private affairs, and I think the gentlemen interested in this enterprise, namely, Messrs. Lash and Mackenzie and Mann, should make an affidavit as to the amount of their personal property over and above their indebtedness, and that amount ought to be risked on their part. It is not fair to ask the people of Canada to keep continually putting up money, unless the men who are as deeply interested, to put it mildly, as we are, dig down into their pockets and .stake every dollar they have to put this enterprise through. The men behind the Canadian Pacific railway did so before they came to the Government asking for a loan of some thirty million dollars. I remember, as a very young man, reading the history of that great undertaking; and even if I thought the methods adopted were all wrong and should have been different from what they were at that time, I always admired the courage of those men who, before they come to the Government for aid, had pledged every dollar they were worth of their personal property, not their collective property as a company, to the banks. Therefore the first thing I would ask i3 that Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann .and Lash, be their property great or toe it small, take their share in this undertaking by pledging every dollar of personal property they have for the completion of this line, and then we shall step in and do something too. Perhaps that is a policy.
Another thing that I think is not unfair- and perhaps there will be differences of opinion in regard to it-is this: The gentlemen interested in the Canadian Northern Railway 'Company have worked hard, it is true. I think, however, they have had some reward. I would not like to say how much or how little, but I think they are able to pay their coal bills anyway, without pinching. But what I do say is that this is not the guarantee of two years ago or three years ago, each of which was supposed to toe final. This is not the guarantee of 1913, which was supposed to be final. This is an extra circumstance under which the Government is appealed to that this pro-fMr. Graham.]
ject must stop unless the Government comes to its rescue, and this is over and above everything else that has been granted, which it was said at the time would complete this great undertaking. The conditions are different from those existing at any time before, because the line is approaching completion, more than half of it having been constructed. Now, the Government, the trustees of the people of Canada, have invested in this road millions of dollars. In putting up the guarantee now proposed, they get no first mortgage on real property. On the other hand, they are guaranteeing every underlying charge against the Canadian Northern Railway system, they are guaranteeing the payment practically of all the indebtedness of the Canadian Northern railway and making sure all the bonds heretofore issued on that line and by subsidiary companies. Under these circumstances, I think it is not unfair that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann should band over, at least for the time being, the control of this enterprise to the Government of Canada. I know theTe are difficulties in the way, from the Government's standpoint, of the Government taking oveT the controlling interest. But as I said before, the conditions are peculiar, the conditions are most exacting; and I do not believe that the people of Canada will be satisfied that at this time their credit should be again extended to the amount of $45,000,000 unless the men who represent them have a controlling voice in the expending of this money. You say to me: We will not allow a dollar to be expended unless in a manner satisfactory to us. I know the routine. This is how it runs: Certain construction takes place on one of the lines, a certain standard of construction being fixed. When this work is done, the company, whichever one it is, comes to the Government with the Government engineer's report, and on this report the money is handed over. It ought to be ' right about face ' under present circumstances. The Government ought to say to the company what work is to be done, what the prices are to be and what money is to be expended before the liability is created, not after the money has been expended. That would make it stronger, that would protect the people who are expecting lines to be built in certain localities not now served by a railway. That would give the Government of Canada the right to say that these lines shall be completed before anything else is undertaken. The Government would have control before

the money is expended, instead of merely confirming each expenditure after it has been made.
But, I am told, we have a man on the board. Well, the Prime Minister, I think, wii'll agree with me that that is not much of a safeguard-I think he will agree with me down in his heart. On the Grand Trunk Pacific they had a board with a Government representative. I have not seen his report for a year or two, but I know that under the old Government there was a man on the board. Well, one man does not form a majority by a great deal.
1 say without any fear of contradiction .that the value to the country of having one man on this board will be absolutely nil so far as the protection of the people of Canada is concerned. The Government has a responsibility, a heavy responsibility. If we are going to give this money or guarantee these bonds, the Government ought to have an amount^ at least equal to what added to their own will form a majority, placed in the hands of trustees, to be automatically handed over to give them control at any moment they like-they ought to have at least that. .My contention is that the Government ought to insist on control until the work is completed and the operation of the Canadian Northern railway begun from ocean to ocean. But I am not unreasonable, I am not an extremist; and if the Government thought it wise to put in a provision that when that time ^arrived that portion which they took to give them control should be disposed of in some other way, I should not object. But, for the present, with the financial condition as it is, when there are attacks .on these great undertakings in Canada, when the work is near completion, when we are dn the particular condition in which we now are, the people of Canada will not be satisfied to give $45,000,000 more of their money to this enterprise unless the people who pay shall control absolutely and directly every dollar of that money.
I think I have made myself clear, but to recapitulate. In the first place, to my mind, the Government has no security, in a practical sense, no security whatever.
In the second place, if they are going to give the money, they might better borrow it and hand it over direct, because they can borrow at a cheaper rate than any company, even with the Government guarantee. This would save millions, and would mean a great deal at this time.
In, the third place, I think that before the resolutions go further the Government ought to have a clause inserted that .Mackenzie, Mann, Lash, or whoever are the stockholders or beneficiaries of these companies, ought to pledge every dollar of their personal property in this undertaking.
Fourth, the Government is not justified in granting aid to the Canadian Northern railway, unless they get control, at least until such time as the enterprise is placed on its feet and the road is in operation.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. J. GARRICK (Thunder Bay and Rainy River):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak of this question not only from the standpoint of the district which I have the honour to represent, but from the larger and more important standpoint of its relation to the Dominion. As the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) said, the problem of railway transportation has been one of the most important questions in Canada since Confederation. In fact, through railways Confederation was made possible and without railways the United Canada that we are so proud of to-day would be only a dream. The Intercolonial united Nova Scotia and New Brunswick with Upper and Lower Canada and its earlier history is replete with the difficulties and hardships of pioneer railway development. Then came the Canadian Pacific project which was for years the all-absorbing political and administrative problem of the time. What other question in Canada has engaged public attention so long? The Government initiated and inaugurated the policy of building the Canadian Pacific railway. Elections were fought and won over this issue alone. It was turned over to a private company which became financially embarrassed and would have failed and gone into liquidation had not the Government of Canada come to its rescue with cash loans and subsidies. And to-day the question of paramount importance throughout Canada is the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern railways. The former we must save and protect, but what are we going to do with the latter?
It may be stated that I am interested. Of course I am interested, and so is everyone in the constituency that I have the honour to represent. If it were not for Mackenzie and Mann and the Canadian Northern railway we would have no Port Arthur as we have it to-day. Only a few years ago Port Arthur was a small hamlet consisting of a mere handful of people and known as Prince Arthur's Landing. It had the lIn the third place, I think that before

honour of being named after our distinguished Royal Governor General. Kail-road construction and development was undertaken and as a direct consequent result we have to-day in the adjoining cities of Port Arthur and Fort William a population of fifty thousand as industrious and prosperous citizens as are to be found in Canada.
If it were not for the railways we would have no Port Arthur or Fort William. The Canadian Pacific railway-the greatest railway system in the world-a national undertaking that we are all proud of-has converted a wilderness into the thriving city of Fort William. The Canadian Pacific railway originally had its lake terminals at Port Arthur, but on account of a dispute with the town officials, who held up an engine for arrears in taxes, it moved its terminals to Fort William, and Sir William Van Horne said that he would make the grass grow in the streets of Port Arthur. The grass did grow in the streets of Port Arthur. Mackenzie and Mann came along and mowed it down; built their railway, and transformed Prince Arthur's Landing into a busy commercial and industrial city which, on account of its geographical location at the head of Canadian navigation- the silvery gateway of the golden West-is destined, especially under this enterprising Government's policy of fostering the iron and steel industry, to be the Chicago of western Canada.
Not only are the citizens of the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William interested in this matter, but the farmers and settlers as well of the surrounding districts are interested. The Canadian Northern railway has opened up and developed the whole Rainy Kiver district. According to Mr. Whitson, Ontario's Good Roads Commissioner, its line traverses the most fertile section of the province of Ontario. Railway development is producing for that district the same beneficial results as were claimed for it in the British House of Commons in 1854, when it was stated that the essence of a railway system is to increase its own traffic, adding twenty-five per cent to the value of every farm within fifty miles of the track; doubling the value of those near the track and quadrupling the value of the farms in the district through which it passes. Interest in this matter is not merely local; it applies not only to Port Arthur and Fort William, but to all the cities and towns which are tributary to this great national highway. It applies more or less 
to every part of the Dominion of Canada. Not only are we interested as individuals; we are interested collectively, for the provinces, from Quebec to British Columbia, have all guaranteed the bonds of the Canadian Northern railway. The credit of thousands of individual citizens, the credit of the provinces and the credit of the Dominion is so interwoven with the Canadian Northern railway that the proper solution of the problems affecting its completion is a question of paramount importance to all Canadians.
For many years it has been fully realized and appreciated that railway construction is necessary to the development of Canada. It was an important condition of Confederation that the Intercolonial railway should be built to unite Upper and Lower Canada with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. British Columbia made it a condition of its entry into Confederation that a line of railway should be built to the coast, and the importance of railway construction was so very forcibly impressed upon the British House of Commons that they guaranteed the bonds of the Intercolonial to the extent of $15,000,000. It has been the long-accepted policy of all political parties and of Canadian Governments to assist and foster railway development. The Conservative party jealously takes credit for the Canadian Pacific railway and the Liberal party for the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, but until this resolution was introduced, no one seemed to want to father the Canadian Northern railway. It is true that this road was conceived and born under the Liberal regime; it is the elder brother of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, but the laws of primogeniture did not prevail, and the Grand * Trunk Pacific railway, with its aristocratic godfather living in London, was the younger and favoured son and received the blessing and inheritance of the Liberal chieftain, while the less fortunate brother was left to struggle alone in a cold, hard world. That is why the newspapers sometimes refer to Bill and Dan as Canada's two lone orphans. As I said, it has long been the policy of the Canadian Government to foster and stimulate rail- . way development, because Canada's prosperity is intertwined with its network of railways, and through its arteries pulsates the industrial life of our commercial existence.
Why not assist in the completion of this great national enterprise at the present time ? Have Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann used the funds which they have procured

through the sale of iheir debentures for the construction of the road, or have they diverted the money to other purposes ? Have they devoted the Canadian Northern railway funds to Mexican, Brazilian or street railway purposes ? Have they used the credit of Canada and the credit of the provinces for their own personal emolument ? Have they made large fortunes for themselves out of the proceeds of railway issues ? These, Mr. Speaker, are questions which the public w'ant answered. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann have presented a full statement to the Government. The Government have appointed, I understand, a com- -mittee of the Cabinet to investigate the matter fully. The Government have asked their railway experts, under the able guidance of Mr. Gutelius, to conduct an investigation. The legal part of the matter was entrusted to the hon. Solicitor General, and I think we are all proud of the agreement which he has made. Expert accountants and auditors have been sent to Toronto to look into the books, and what do they find ? They find that every dollar that has been raised by the debenture issues guaranteed by the provinces and the Dominion has gone into the construction of the road and that not one single dollar of Canadian Northern railway funds has gone into Mexican, Brazilian or street railway operations. They find further that nearly $100,000,000 not guaranteed by the provinces and the Dominion has all gone into the construction of this railway, and they find that Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann have not taken for their services the money to which they are justly entitled. According to the affidavit recently made by Mr. A. J. Mitchell, comptroller of the company, since the road assumed the proportions of a transcontinental system, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann have taken no profits out of the company, save and except certain common stock. What else do they find? They find that these men devoted their own personal resources and their own assets to the building of this road; that they turned over to the company 4,000,000 acres of land grants which they secured in respect of the Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company, the Manitoba and Southeastern Railway Company, and the Winnipeg and Hudson Bay Railway Company, which under the terms of the charters became their own personal property upon completion of the railways. Part of these lands have already been sold for $17,000,000, and the remainder is worth, at the prevailing
price of adjoining lands, $13,000,000. This money, to which the contractors were personally entitled, has now become part of and is included in the assets of the Canadian Northern railway. They turned their lands and the proceeds of sales over to the railway company without receiving a single dollar in return, and they also turned over d great number of other assets which belonged to the Mackenzie and Mann Company, such . as transport contracts, Lake Superior terminals at Port Arthur, elevators, docks, holdings of the Canadian Northern Telegraph Company, the Canadian Northern Express Company, the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake Railway Company, the Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific Railway Company, the Port Arthur, Duluth and Western Railway Company, and the St. Boniface and Western Land Company. According to the statement presented, these assets are worth $50,000,000. What did they receive for these cash assets? They received common stock, which is not worth one dollar unless the railway is a success. Does this look as if the object of Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann was to exploit railroad building in Canada, to exploit the credit of the provinces and to exploit the credit of the Dominion for their own personal gain? No, Mr. Speaker; if their object had been personal gain and personal emolument they would not have turned over to the Canadian Northern Railway Company millions of dollars in land grants, transport contracts, elevators and telegraph and express companies. No, Mr. Speaker; they have a higher and a worthier ambition; not an inordinate ambition for personal gain or personal enrichment, but an ambition as Canadian-born citizens to develop Canada and to leave behind them a monument that will transmit their memory to posterity and redound to the credit of Canada. Small minds cannot appreciate high motives, but, let me ask whether Sir John A. Macdonald devoted a life to service to Canada for personal gain? Has the right hon. leader of the Opposition devoted forty years of his life to Canada for personal emolument? Is the present Prime Minister devoting every energy, every ability, and every faculty with which he is endowed to the service of his country for the sake of personal gain? Is there not a loftier, higher and nobler ambition among our great men? Sir, there is, and as Canadians we are proud to acknowledge it. Our public men of to-day are just as capable of disinterested endeavours, noble conceptions and self-sacrifices as

were the splendid characters that adorn the pages of our history. Let us not be ungenerous in the motives we assign to two of our greatest Canadians, Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann.	.
Who are the detractors of these two distinguished Canadians? I am very sorry for the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), and I regret that he is not in his seat that I might express my personal sympathy with him in his unfortunate position. Disappointment in politics is somethng like disappointment in love: it is liable to embitter the sweetest and most amiable disposition and turn the vials of wrath upon one's own party and associates. At the present time the province of Alberta has no representative in the Cabinet, which is a bitter disappointment to the would-be Cabinet minister from Calgary. One could see by his speech in the House that bitter jealousy animated his personal attitude towards the Solicitor General, because he himself was anxious for that position. What a source of strength he would have been to the Cabinet!
He said, two or three weeks ago, that when he made his speech in the Commons, the Government dare not give any assistance of the Canadian Northern railway; the stampede would be transferred from Calgary to Ottawa and the bucking broncho would kick down all the Government bars and create consternation in the camp. The words of the dramatist are very appropriate when he says:
But man, proud man!
Brest in a little brief authority,
Plays such fantastic tricks before high Heaven
As make the angels weep.
It is the irony of fate that we should be sent down here to follow Mr. Borden and not a bucking broncho from the West. What an anomalous position for the bon. gentleman to fulfil, to be a back-bencher with would-be Cabinet aspirations, and how amazing it is that the Government has beep able to get on without such a great railway authority, the greatest living railway expert out of captivity. Here the dramatist again describes him:
What a piece of work man is ! how noble in reason! how infinite in faculty, in form and moving how express and admirable! in action how like an angel! in apprehension how like a god !
I understand that there has been a new party formed called the Bull Moose party; that the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) is the leader, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) the first lieuten-[Mr Carrick. ]
ant. I understand that the hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Hepburn) was unanimously elected chief whip of the Bull Moose party; but after full consideration and much talk he declined the honour, deciding that it would be better to remain a barnacle on the good old ship of state. Like Horatius of old, Theodore the Second then cried:
Who will stand on my left hand
And keep the bridge with me?
And up stepped Don Quixote, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins), but, after taking a good look at the Government forces, he decided that discretion was the better part of valour; whereupon he purchased a ticket to parts unknown, sanctimoniously remarking to his three associates in caucus assembled:
He who fights and runs away
May live to fight another day.
What is the business side of the proposition? The Toronto Globe discussed it editorially, and said that it was quite natural that the competing companies did not want the Government to assist the Canadian Northern railway. It also stated that the Canadian Northern railway, whilst yet an uncompleted road, had saved the farmers of this country on grain shipments alone $17,000,000 by the reduction of freight rates, and had saved to the shippers of the Dominion of Canada a total of $50,000,000. Part of this editorial was read this morning by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr Bristol), but another part was not; so I will read the entire editorial. It is as follows:
The suggestion that opponents of the Canadian Northern railway raid on Ottawa are ' playing the game ' of the Canadian Pacific railway is most unworthy. The Canadian Pacific railway is playing its own game openly and above board. The Canadian Northern railway promises to become a powerful rival of the original transcontinental. It may prove a much more effective competitor than it otherwise could hope to be if the Government of Canada continues to provide the money or pledge the credit of the people for its completion and up-to-date equipment. Were any other shrewd business man in Sir Thomas Shaugh-nessy's place he would probably protest as vigorously as the president of the Canadian Pacific against further aid to the Canadian Northern railway.
Sir Thomas is actuated by an Intelligent selfishness and conveniently forgets that the Canadian Pacific railway during the construction stage usually paid dividends upon the common stock out of moneys that should have gone to construction; that the North American Construction Company, composed of directors and officials, occupied the position of favoured con-

will become one of the great national highways of Canada.
Ever since Confederation there has been a popular demand for railways. The different provinces have been eager for colonization roads to open up and develop their respective provinces. They have been vying with each other for railway development. Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have all given subsidies or bond guarantees to the Canadian Northern railway, and the Dominion Government has given both. They did not give assistance simply to satisfy a whim of Mackenzie and Mann to build railways. They gave assistance because the people wanted and demanded railways. The provinces asked and solicited Mackenzie and Mann to build through districts where it will be years before the returns are commensurate with the investment. They have built through my constituency from Port Arthur to Sudbury, a distance of 500 miles. The line traverses the great clay belt of New Ontario, consisting of sixteen million acres of as fertile agricultural land as can be found in Canada; but which according to Ontario's Commission of 1900 is a territory larger than the states of Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Jersey and Delaware combined', and nearly all of which is well adapted for cultivation, with a climate not much different from that of the province of Manitoba. The territory possesses an abundance of wood for fuel, building and commercial purposes, and many falls on the rivers and streams, which may be used with advantage in the creation of electrical energy "when the country comes to be opened up.
The Ontario Government Commissioners estimated that in the district of Nipissing there were at least twenty million cords of pulpwood; in Algoma, one hundred million ; and the Thunder Bay, one hundred and fifty million; a total of two hundred and seventy million cords of pulp-wood. In addition there is a very considerable quantity of merchantable pine timber.
The district immediately adjoining Sudbury contains the largest known deposits of nickle, and is to-day the world's centre of the nickle industry. There are many millions of tons of iron ore deposits in this northern country. We have heard ior years and years of the great undeveloped resources of Canada and this phrase has a very pleasing sound; but Canadians cannot afford to live much longer with the charge that they have great undeveloped re-
sources. That which was once a boast has become almost a reflection on our national character. The Government of Canada has a trust to perform and that trust lies in the development of our natural resources, and the first step towards development is transportation. This great clay belt belongs to the people of Canada. Without railway facilities, it is of very little value; with railways, it is worth millions of dollars. There is no settlement in this district yet; no local traffic to help pay the interest on the bonds. But, in a few years, this great agricultural clay belt will'be settled with prosperous farmers; towns will spring up and the products of the farm will be exchanged for the wares of the artisan to the mutual advantage of both. In the meantime Mackenzie and Mann have built the railway and are carrying the burden, while the benefit of opening np the country and the enhancement in the value of the land inures to the credit of the people of Canada. Surely none of the provinces, or the Dominion, will take the position that they granted assistance simply at the solicitation of Mackenzie and Mann. They gave assistance at the solicitation and demand of the people to open up the country and provide railway facilities; and in the present application of Mackenzie and Mann this should receive every consideration.
What about the physical character of the Canadian Northern railway? Has it a good road bbd? Is it well constructed? It is very difficult to compare railway systems from the standpoint of cost and expenditure. This has been amply demonstrated in the recent lengthy debate on the Grand Trunk Pacific railway when numerous figures were given showing comparative costs of different systems. Date of construction, nature of territory, wages paid, rate of interest and general economic conditions, are all contributing factors in computing cost. Without giving interminable figures I think it can be readily shown that the Canadian Northern Railway system has cost less per mile than any other system in Canada; and at the same time, in order to receive the subsidies, it has been built to the very high standard required by Dominion Government specifications. What does this mean to Canada? It means, if cost of construction is a factor in determining tariff rates, that the Canadian Northern railway when completed will be instrumental in reducing rates throughout Canada; and according to the Globe this railway, while yet uncompleted, has already reduced rates and saved

the farmers of western Canada $17,000,000 on grain alone, and a total of $50,000,000 to the shippers of Canada in the last ten years.
Last year I travelled over the Canadian Northern railway from Port Arthur to Winnipeg, a distance of 438 miles, and our running time for the whole distance averaged over fifty miles an hour. This rate could not be maintained over a poorly constructed line, and I think the roadbed and equipment can compare favourably with any other road in western Canada. Mr. Angus Sinclair, who is a well known civil engineer and contractor and familiar with the whole Canadian Northern system says:
When the system Is completed, with its easy grades and curvatures, its completely new equipment, and Its high standard of construction, it will be without exception the finest railway in America.
When Sir Richard McBride was in Ottawa recently he stated in an interview that there is no better road in the whole of British Columbia.
The Canadian Northern railway crosses the Rocky mountains through the Yellow-head pass at the lowest grade line on the American continent. The Union Pacific crosses the Rocky mountains at a height of 8,000 feet, with a grade of 2i per cent; the Northern Pacific at 7,000 feet; the Great Northern at 6,000 feet; the Canadian Pacific main line at 5,300 feet; the Canadian Pacific Crow's Nest Pass line at 4,300 feet; the Canadian Northern at 3,700 feet. The Canadian Pacific maximum grade through the Rockies is 2.2 per cent; the Great Northern 2 per cent; the Grand Trunk Pacific 1 per cent, and the Canadian Northern 7-10th of 1 per cent. So the Canadian Northern crosses the Rockies at the lowest and best grade on the whole American continent, and thus has a great advantage over competing systems.
What is the nature cf the country that the Canadian Northern traverses? Mr. S. J. McLean, railway commissioner, in his article on national highways, says that the Canadian Northern is built through the most fertile wheat sections in western Canada, and this fact is amply demonstrated by last year's statistics, which show that it carried nearly one-third of the grain shipped from the West to the lake ports of Port Arthur and Fort William.
Mr. Speaker, I think Mackenzie and Mann are entitled to the earnest consideration of this Government. During the past twenty years they have been one of the greatest factors in the development and
prosperity of Canada. They have brought to Canada, and expended in Canadian development, over three hundred millions of dollars. They have built railroads and colonization branches at the request and solicitation of the provinces and the Dominion. They have given employment, directly and indirectly, to hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens. Their monthly pay roll runs into millions of dollars. They have saved the people of Canada in freight rates in the past ten .years $50,000,000. Where can we find two other Canadians with such a record? They are the greatest all-star team that has ever been produced in Canada. One is a past master in the art of finance; the other a past master in the art of construction. I happened to be in the old country last year when they were on their annual quest for money. Times were very hard and money difficult to secure. A Canadian, Sir Max Aitken, expressed the general feeling in England when he said it was most important to Canada for Sir William to get money for the Canadian Northern. Leading British financiers said he could not get it; but he did get it, and then they said no man could have got it but Sir William Mackenzie. No man in London has the confidence of the financial interests to a greater degree, because he has always faithfully and honourably discharged all his obligations and every time they exchange their gold for his securities they give him another certificate of sterling integrity and honour of which the Canadian people should be proud.
And, Mr. Speaker, the characteristic traits as exemplified in our two distinguished Canadians-power of initiative, capacity for work, sterling integrity and character- constitute the most precious heritage of any people; and I am firmly convinced that it is this asset, intangible if you will, that has placed Canada in the position she occupies among civilized nations. For, in the last analysis, it is not wealth, natural resources, material things, that make a nation, but it is the virility and national characteristic traits of the men born and bred in a country that, in the final court of appeal, determine its status. Capacity and character must be fostered and stimulated before our natural resources can be developed and great achievements accomplished.
In conclusion, I believe it will greatly redound to the credit of Canada to enable Mackenzie and Mann to finish their railway

system. They are Canadian born citizens who are building for the benefit of Canada, and it is truly stated in the preamble of their charter that the work is for the general advantage of Canada. It is Canada, not Mackenzie and Mann, that gains or loses by any assistance the Government may or may not give. They have not sought-their own personal gain and emolument, by withholding land grants, elevators, town-sites, but have a higher and nobler ambition, and any assistance we can give at the present time will redound to the credit of this Government and the people of Canada as it redounded to the credit of Canada under Sir John A. Macdonald's Government when he came to the rescue of the Canadian Pacific railway and enabled that company to complete its road. Mr. Speaker,
I congratulate this Government upon rising to the occasion, protecting the fair name and credit of Canada and helping complete this great national highway.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Carrick) is always listened to with pleasure on the all too rare occasions upon which he addresses the House. His enthusiasm for this proposition is natural and genuine, but I am free to say that I think the conditions under which my hon. friend approached this subject are such that he can hardly be said to apply to its consideration that keen business judgment which is usually inseparable from him in other matters. We are in a peculiar position in the consideration of this measure. We have had the spectacle, within the last two days, of two of the cleverest young publie men in this country supporting the Government, openly declaring that upon a -very fundamental and important proposition, the legislation submitted by the Government to the House, they are unable to support that Government and that they have decided to vote against the proposition. Differences in regard to public matters may sometimes exist under the system of party government, but it has rarely occurred in the history of this Parliament that men possessing the integrity and occupying a position in which they can be said to be absolutely disinterested in their view, have broken away from all those ties that have carried them along in life hitherto and have taken a position of antagonism to everything with which they have up to the present time been associated. The indictment which these hon. gentlemen presented to this House, in giv-

ing the reasons why this measure should not receive the support of this Parliament and of the country, were of such serious and grave import that I submit that this Government cannot disregard them, that this House cannot fail to direct attention to them, and that the country will be awakened by so serious a proposition as that which the Government are submitting to Parliament at the present time.
When we have such a situa-5 p.m. tion in regard to the matter as is presented in reference to this Canadian Northern Railway proposition, in view of the history which is familiar to every one of us, in view of the events of last year when gentlemen representing the Canadian Northern railway came to the Prime Minister of the country and said to him: If you will only give us #15,000,000 we can complete this third transcontinental railway; when the Prime Minister of this country, on the faith ef that statement, stood up in this House and justified to his friends and to the country a presentation of this measure to Parliament by the statement made by such an authority that the great railway would be completed if this aid were given; when we find that that statement was absolutely and unqualifiedly untrue, we have a condition that warrants the strong language which was adopted in this House by the two hon. gentlemen supporting this Government to whom I have referred. But when you have the hon. the Finance Minister (Mr. White), as he did last year, disregarding all the appeals which were made to him from this side of the House to stop and investigate the financial position of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, to make an inquiry into their assets, their liabilities, and their standing in Canada and elsewhere before he purchased #7,000,000 of their stock and paid them #15,000,000 of Canadian money therefor, when you find the Minister of Finance absolutely disregarding all these entreaties and stating that, as he had been informed, if the aid that was then proposed was given, the whole system would be completed by the year 1914, and when we find in one short year afterwards these two hon. gentlemen coming back to this House to admit that they were deceived, to admit that they should have investigated, to admit that they should have gone into the situation of the Canadian Northern railway with the greatest possible care and exactitude last year, and that because they did not do so the Government, the House and the country were deceived, you, Sir,

will agree with me that when these gentlemen come back to this House and ask us to go into a partnership with the men and with the enterprise which indulged in, that fraudulent misrepresentation, to use the language of my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett), we have a curious spectacle indeed. As to the deceit, there can be no question. My hon. friend from Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), who is the amicus curiae, the man outside but still within the confidence of the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden), who leads this House, to whom has been committed some of the influence possessed by hon. gentlemen who have seats in the Cabinet, who, from time to time on important questions, gives the House his suggestions as to what our friends opposite would do, and which he has always done since this Government came into office, said yesterday in the apology -not the argument-which he presented in regard to this measure, and it is as well that we should recall it, because it was language of great significance:
Those of us who remember the legislation of last session, when we were given to understand that the aid then advanced would mean the completion of the road and that nothing further would be demanded, while we feel that those who made those representations in this House were sincere in believing that the evidence laid before them was in accordance with the facts, cannot help feeling that to some extent they were deceived, and purposly deceived,-
Mark the significance of the language.
-and that this House acted on a supposition which further events have shown to be unfounded. Therefore, we cannot altogether get away from a feeling of annoyance at the way in which we were treated.
The mild and gentle member for St. Antoine, strong and faithful party man as he is, mustered up sufficient courage in his apology for this measure to suggest that we could not help getting a little bit annoyed over this deception. Is the House to be content simply with this mild expresision of annoyance? When we are proposing to form a positive and lasting partnership with the Canadian Northern railway, under which we bind ourselves, if not in a bond, yet in absolute reality to furnish all the finances that this company will require to complete this enterprise, are we to content ourselves with being somewhat annoyed at being deceived; or is my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) right when he declares that, before Parliament enters into a partnership with these gentlemen, there should be a full and complete investigation into all the circumstances connected
with this enterprise, so that we may find out why that misrepresentation was made last year.
I am sure the House was struck with the fact-and the country is not aware of it yet -that, when Mackenzie and Mann came to this Government with the stock for which they paid $210 for every $100 last year, instead of giving to the Government of this country $7,000,000 out of the $70,000,000 worth of stock that was supposed to have been issued, they proceeded to issue $7,000,000 more stock. To use the somewhat extreme language of my hon. friend from Calgary, they started a printing press and rolled [DOT] off $7,000,000 more stock, and gave it to the unsuspecting Minister of Finance, who did not know that he was getting this new stock that was being issued to him, but who thought, in all his childish innocence, that he was getting $7,000,000 out of the $70,000,000. Not until the autumn did he discover that he had been sold like a child by these great financiers, who had buncoed him by giving him this $7,000,000 worth of stock which was never issued until they ran it in the printing press.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance is asking this Parliament to reimburse the men who invested in the Farmers Bank certain sums of money as deposits, alleging an error in judgment on the part of the previous Minister of Finance. I venture to say there has never been a Minister of Finance since Confederation who has been guilty of such gross negligence and disregard of the interest of Canada as the present Minister of Finance was when he allowed himself to be deceived by these people last year, and when he allowed them to palm off on him this $7,000,000 worth of stock that never existed until the printing press was started once more. Is it any wonder that my hon. friend from St. Antoine is. somewhat annoyed? Is it any wonder that even he, while he cannot permit himself to take the stern position which his friends from Calgary and Kingston have taken, is bound to express dissatisfaction with such conduct and to indicate to the House and to the country that he is swallowing this dose of medicine with a very bad grace? '
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance did not care to have anything to do with these people. What are the facts in regard to the situation this session? Everybody who has been in Ottawa since the session began knows that, when Mackenzie and Mann came here in February looking for aid, the word went up and down that no

aid was to be given. It was stated that hon. gentlemen in the Government had declared that Mackenzie and Mann might as well go into bankruptcy now as three years from now. After Sir William Mackenzie had consulted the Minister of Finance and gone back to Toronto and given an interview to a paper, in which he said that he had made a presentation to the Government for aid, we had the spectacle of the hon. Minister of Finance declaring in this House that nothing of the kind had happened. I refer to ' Hansard ' of March 3, when my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition had called the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance to what Sir William Mackenzie had said. The Minister of Finance, who was smarting under, and who is still smarting under, the deception practised on him last year, and who has handed over to the youthful Solicitor General the task of being toyed with by that shrewd legal genius, Zebulon A. Nash, because he does not want to run the risk of being toyed with this year, on the 3rd of March replied to the right hon. leader of the Opposition as follows:
Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) : X can give an explanation of the statement which I made to the press, but as to the statement of Sir William Mackenzie, or as to any remarks that may he attributed to him, of course I cannot speak. My hon. friend has correctly read what X stated to the press, namely, that no application had been received for assistance by way of loan to any railway company, nor was any expected to be received. So far as I am aware, that is a correct statement of the facts.
Mr. hon. friend the Minister olf Finance was clearly annoyed, like the member for St. Antoine, over the situation of last year. Hon. members will note that up-to-date he has had nothing whatever to do with the matter. Newer and cruder hands have been given the task of initiating this country into partnership with Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann.
After it was clearly understood that no further aid was to be given, it was said: But Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann owe $21,000,000 to people in this country; to carmen, to railway contractors, to men who have worked with the spade and shovel out in the northlands, and these poor fellows will be destitute unless Parliament intervenes. But insidiously were the outworks pushed forward until there came to be a feeling quite clearly existing in the arena of the House that, after all, perhaps it would be better to do something for these poor fellows who were entitled to their money. Al-

though there was created in the ranks of my right hon. friend a feeling of sympathy and that something ought to be done in that regard, the ridiculous part of the matter is that there is no provision, as I shall show, in these resolutions for the payment of that $21,000,000 to the railroad contractors and to the men who have sold materials to this railway.
The Minister of Finance, on March 3, said that there had been no application for a loan; that there was nothing doing. In the blue-book which has been brought down, I find the following letter:
Ottawa, March 5, 19X4. To the Xtight Honourable It. D. Borden, Premier of Canada.
Dear Sir,-For the reasons mentioned in the memoranda and statements respecting the Canadian Northern Railway system, submitted it is essential that the company should receive further Government aid. The amount required is forty-two million dollars ($42,000,000).
Recognizing the difficulties in the way of a cash loan, I beg to apply for a guarantee of securities to the extent of forty-five million dollars ($45,000,000), par value. The discount on the disposal of these securities would probably reduce the proceeds below the forty-two million dollars ($42,000,000).
I have the honour to be,
Tour obedient servant,
Wm, Mackenzie,
President-
Now, we are asked to believe that Sir .William Mackenzie came to the Government on the 5th of March, two days after .the Minister of Finance had made his statement to the country, and without any paore data, without more reasons given than the statement to the effect that it was essential-'essential'-that	this money
should be found for him, this Government proceeded to get it. I asked the Prime .Minister a few days ago where was the memorandum that accompanied this letter. He indicated that he thought that the memorandum was contained in these financial statements that have been submitted. But I apprehend from the correspondence attached to the documents that these statements were furnished subsequently to the application being made by Sir William Mackenzie, before the employment of the auditors, and after the Solicitor General had written the correspondence in the latter portion of this book directing what should be done.

The information is
furnished in extremely crude form. Apparently a large part of the knowledge that we are supposed to depend upon is in the head of the Solicitor General, as was indicated by the encounter between that hon. gentleman and the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) yesterday. The information is not of such a character as would warrant Parliament, without further investigation, in entering upon this momentous proposition and becoming a partner in this . great enterprise. If this information about the length of the line, what it cost to build, what is necessary to finish, if that was the . only information Sir William Mackenzie gave when he made this application of the 5th of March, then I say that Sir William Mackenzie gave this Government no information to warrant them in coming to Parliament with these resolutions) even though their auditors verified the statements that he submitted. When Sir William Mackenzie stated to the Prime Minister la^t year that with $15,000,000 he would complete the railway why should he be given more money now for that purpose merely on his statement that it was ' essential ' he should have the money? There was no allegation that he was unable to pay his bills or that he had difficulty in financing in London-no data such as any other enterprise that ever came to Parliament for assistance has been called upon to give. My right hon. friend's great predecessor in the leadership of the Conservative party acted differently in 1884 when the Canadian Pacific railway came asking for relief. The preamble of the Act by which that relief was granted sets out in detail the reasons why Parliament was asked for this aid-ample and sufficient reasons, if they were true, why Parliament should interfere. Compare with this, the one statement on the part of Sir William Mackenzie that it was ' essential ' for him to get the money, and that my right hon. friend should take the step he does on that statement seems ludicrous and incomprehensible. It is no wonder that his supporters from Kingston 241
and Calgary should leave him on this question. Here is the preamble of the Bill of 1884:
Whereas the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have represented, that although possessed of property and assets, which, if realized, would be sufficient for the completion of the Canadian Pacific railway w'ithin one-half of the time contemplated by the contract between the Government and the company, namely, by the first day of May, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-six, yet that in consequence of the state of the market for railway securities, and of other circumstances beyond their control, and notwithstanding the agreement made with the Government on the seventh day of November last, for securing for ten years from the seventeenth day of August last, a three per centum dividend upon their outstanding stock, they are unable to procure the funds required for proceeding with the work of construction as rapidly as is necessary to complete the railway within the said earlier period, and have applied for certain modifications of the contract of construction and of the said agreement, and for an advance upon the security of their entire railway, branches, equipment and property in order to assist them in so proceeding with such work; and whereas it is expedient, in furtherance of the early settlement of the Northwest territories and of the completion of transcontinental communication by railway through Canada, that the early completion of the said railway should be ensured: Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
But this document of the 5th of March contains no such allegations. One hon. gentleman tells us that this company will go into liquidation if this money is not provided. But the Solicitor General-I think it was-argued that that was not the state of affairs at all, but that so far as the Canadian Northern railway was concerned and so far as Mackenzie and Mann were concerned, they had ample funds but that it was the duty of the country in the premises to assist in this enterprise. When we look at the preamble of the resolution which my right hon. friend introduced, we find that he simply alleged that:
Whereas the Canadian Northern Railway Company hereinafter called the ' Canadian Northern ' has represented that the several companies set forth in the first schedule to these resolutions, and their railways and undertakings, rolling stock, equipment, assets and properties are intended to constitute a transcontinental railway system to be denominated the 4 Canadian Northern System ' and that the Canadian Northern desires to control said system by the ownership or control of the shares or majorities thereof in the capital stock of the said companies, and that it now own or controls the shares or majorities thereof in the capital stock of certain of the said companies, and that the several companies are desirous that aid should be granted for the purpose of completing the construction and equipment of the works and undertakings of the Canadian



Northern system and for the betterment thereof.
That is all. Mark the difference between the way Sir John Macdonald proceeded in 1884-Sir John Macdonald, whose name and record, my hon. friend from Rainy River (Mr. Carrick) invoked, and the method by which the present leader has proceeded in the matter in which he is handing out $45,000,000 more of money with lesser security, and is embarking in a partnership venture under which Canada makes herself liable in addition for $312,000,000 that we know of and for other millions the number of which nobody can yet estimate.
Now, it was essential that Sir William Mackenzie get this aid. The Minister of Finance (Mr. White) did not want to have anything to do with it, so the task was given to my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). And that hon. gentleman received his first lesson in how to draw up a railway contract from Mr. Z. A. Lash. On the one side is my hon. friend acting for the Government and on the other that astute railway lawyer, who has been drawing contracts, agreements and trust deeds of the most artistic shapes all his life. Indeed, I have heard of several members of the Bar who have not had the opportunity of seeing a trust deed such as Mr. Z. A. Lash could draw until they were placed on the table, taking them home to . preserve them for examination and record and for the instruction of students in various portions of the Dominion. That astute railway solicitor, who has ploughed through many a stormy sea of litigation and difficulty, was put up to make an agreement with my hon. friend the Solicitor	General-and he took the hon.
gentleman into camp in splendid shape. That is what was to be expected. The Solicitor General has had his head turned since he got into that office. He is being touted and talked of all over the country- the Federal News Bulletin circulating its half-page photograph and biography of this Daniel come to judgment whose deliverance on the Transcontinental put even my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) in the shade-why even the Prime Minister and every other hon. gentleman on that side are paling into insignificance before this new light that has come. When he rose the other night we thought that he was going to explain to the House this wonderful agreement that he had made with Mr. Z. A. Lash, who, being one of the noble eighteen, would be supposed to have special influence with this Government.

But, instead of explaining the agreement, the hon. gentleman chided the right hon. leader of the Opposition because he did not know all about it. The Solicitor General was the only one who did know all about it, and he found fault with my hon. friend, saying:	You admit
the necessity and the desirability of completing a third transcontinental railway, and you propose to give these people a certain amount of money by way of loan without any security. It does seem to me that a gentleman having the aspirations possessed by the hon. Solicitor General should, in dealing with questions of this kind, approach their consideration upon some basis of fairness. If you refer to my hon. friend's assertion you will find that he reiterated the charge that the right hon. leader of the Opposition proposed to loan this money without taking any security whatever. This is what he said:
If it appears to the leader of the opposition that the Canadian Northern Railway Company were not at the present time ahle to carry on their enterprises without assistance, he would loan them the money out of the treasury of the country and he would take no compensation in return.
That is not what my right hon. friend said at all. My right hon. friend said that ho would deal with the matter as Sir John A. Macdonald dealt with the Canadian Pacific railway in 1884. Yet the hon. Solicitor General, carried away by the applause of hon. gentlemen opposite, some of whom have never read the agreement, reiterated the statement that the leader of the Opposition was proposing to give this money without any compensation whatever. If my hon. friend the Solicitor General had followed the lines of the agreement made in 1884 with the Canadian Pacific railway he would not have been compelled to submit to the desertion of two distinguished members of 'his party, the hon. member for Calgary and the hon. member for Kingston. Had my ben. friend the Solicitor General attempted in any court in this country to make a case on such a statement as he made to this House with regard to the merits of this proposed agreement, any judge would decide against him on his opening. Outside of what the hon. Solicitor General has said, what information has been given to this House and the country with regard to the proposed agreement? Who has answered the assertions of the hon. member for Kingston and the hon. member for Calgary? The House still waits

for some hon. gentleman on the other side to deal with this question, if it can be dealt with, in some practical way, in order that we may know, at least, what the view of the Government is in regard to it.
My hon. friend failed to explain who was going to pay this $21,000,000. I made the statement that the one and only reason why there developed in this House a sympathy for this Canadian Northern proposition was the theory that there was $21,000,000 owed throughout this land and that it was not fair that the people who claimed this money should be without it. What is the situation? I wish to give some figures, and I hope the hon. Solicitor General will correct me if I am wrong. I find, in going through the return which has been brought down- I have not the advantage of any private information, as my hon. friend has-that the financial condition . of the Canadian Northern people to-day is this: as shown on page 43 of the blue book, their floating liabilities amount to $10,408,128. As shown on page 42, the amount due on construction is $21,262,527. As shown on page 10, they require $41,905,117 to complete the construction of the railway. Then, we have the further indebtedness to the banks of this country, which was exposed by my right hon. friend and leader, to the amount of $20,703,865.
Where is that to be found?

It is not in the
printed books, but it is in the statement which the right hon. leader of the Opposition found in the return and which was admitted in the discussion a few days ago. The figures which I have given make a total indebtedness of $94,279,637.56.
Will the hon.. gentleman give the figures again ? I do not see how he makes the $94,000,000.
Floating liabilities, $10,000,000; due on construction, $21,262,000; balance necessary for completion, $41,905,000.
That is not a liability.

I am speaking of the amount of money which this company requires in order to complete the railway, and I am including in that the liabilities which exist to-day and the amount of money which they state they require, after giving credit for all the assets set out on page 9 of the blue-book. I add to that $20,703,000, the amount which is owing. to the banks, and I make a total of $94,279,637. It is
stated that $24,000,000 are pledged to the company as security for this $21,000,000. Supposing these securities have a par value; there would be to the credit of the company, coming from the banks, $3,396,135.

books-
