I want to ask my hon. friend the Solicitor General to lay upon the table of the House at once a statement of the securities that have been pledged to the banks and what their normal value is.	.
It is tabled.

It is not in the books. If there is a statement tabled, I have no doubt that the hon. member for Calgary and the hon. member for Kingston had it, in view of their speeches of yesterday. At any rate, it was rather difficult for hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to get it.
If I may explain-
My hon. friend will tell me this: At what does he value the securities that are pledged to the banks?
I will get that in a moment. In the meantime, let me say that everything was printed that was asked to be printed; the rest was laid on the table of the House.
I am asking my hon. friend only one question.
I have a right to say that, whether my hon. friend desires it or not.

My hon. friend has a right to say nothing which I do not permit him to say during the course of my speech; he may as well understand that. I asked my hon. friend what he gives as the value of the securities now pledged to the banks for the loan of $20,000,000?

$24,324,029.10. The
price of each one is given in the statement.
Then my hon. friend need not have corrected me, because I was .giving him exactly that amount.
That is correct, but it is not on a par value.

Whether or not it is On a par value, is entirely unimportant; what we want to get at is the actual value. From what my hon. friend says, it can be seen that there is a margin of $3,396,135 over and above the amount owing to the banks. I deduct that $3,396,000 from the $94,000,000, which shows that, taking into consideration the $41,000,000 necessary to complete the road, the Canadian Northern enterprise, or the Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, require $90,000,000 to pay their debts and to complete the road, after making allowances for all the securities which are credited on page 10 of the blue book. My hon. friend apparently agrees with that. If they require $90,000,00 to complete the road, this country is only giving them one-half of that amount, $45,000,000, and the net value of that $45,000,000 is $42,000,000, which means that there is $48,000,000 of debt and of money necessary for the completion of the road that have to be found somewhere. Where does my hon. friend in this agreement provide for that? We find first, in regard to this money owing to the banks, that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, or the Canadian Northern railway, undertake that that $20,000,000 will be paid out of $24,000,000 of securities that have been put by. So we will assume that one crosses the other. Then, in regard to floating liability, we have the covenant here that Mackenzie and Mann themselves will, within one year, retire or reduce that $10,000,000 down to a floating amount, in the judgment of the Government. We will assume that they can do that, but where does my hon. [DOT]friend find $21,262,000 to pay the implement men, the contractors and sub-contractors and the men who worked with the pick and shovel all over the country? Where does my hon. friend say they are going to get that?

They get the proceeds of $45,000,000 of the guaranteed securities; but, in addition to that, they have, in unsold and unearned securities, $58,000,000 besides, which totals $100,000,000 odd. In

that $100,000,000 odd the $21,000,000 is included, and consequently the $21,000,000 must be got out of those two. .
My hon. friend says that out of this $58,000,000 of securities that exist the $21,000,000 is going to be paid?
Out of the $45,000,000.
Does my hon. friend say that this $21,000,000 of debt is included in the statement of requirements to complete on page 10?
I do not know about the page, hut there is a total of $100,000,000. Yes, it is included in that $100,379,099.

How can that be? Take, for instance, equipment. There is owing for general equipment $1,539,863. The only item for equipment on page 10 is item No. 5, rolling stock, equipment for transcontinental, and maturing equipment notes, $27,000,000. Will my hon. friend say that the $1,539,863 is included in the $27,000,000?
Yes, and the whole $21,000,000 is included, spread over these items.
Has my hon. friend any statement showing that?
Yes, I have -seen a statement, I am pretty sure it is filed. I can produce it to you.
It is as well that my hon. friend should personally undertake to give it to me.
Yes.

Because I am interested in the case of those to whom this money is owing. I want to know whether they will get the money out of the $45,000,000 the Government are going to give them, or where they are going to get it.

The indebtedness of
$21,262,000 is to be liquidated out of the $45,000,000 and the $58,000,000. I cannot say in what proportion it will be, but it must be done out of both, if that is the way it is to go.

Does my hon. friend, for the Government, say that it will be the business of the Government, under this clause which gives control of the payment out of this money, to see that these men to whom this money is now owing will be paid?

The Government follow this money to destination and the Govern-

ment only have control of the $45,000,000 and of such proportion of the other as is guaranteed by the Government. The Government will see that that money, so under its control, goes first to debts. Now, on the other hand, there will be a proportion of debt doubtless that will be applicable to the unguaranteed securities but which will be paid in due course without question before the non-guaranteed securities and the Government securities are expended.

There are people in
this country who are owed money by the Canadian Northern railway whose claims are included in the $21,000,000. We have seen them around this Parliament, and they have told members of Parliament that there are people suffering financially today by reason of the fact that they have not received their money from the Canadian Northern railway. The condition of affairs is this, if I understand my hon. friend aright. This Government are giving securities which will net $42,000,000. Will he undertake to say that one-half of that amount will go to pay those debts or will he not?
I have made the statement as clearly as I can make it, that is always in the power of the Government.

The Government declines to give and absolute assurance upon this question and I want to say that hon. gentlemen in this House know that were it not for the representations made here and throughout the country that it was necessary to make this advance in order that the people who were owed this money would get it, this Government would never have had the temerity to come to this Parliament, in view of the opposition which has been exhibited from their own friends. And it also shows, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that the $45,000,000 of security, to which the country ip being committed under this measure, is but the beginning of further and much greater grants which of necessity will have to be made by this governmental partner of this railway. My hon. friend the other night, in dealing with this question, evaded the point with skill. He declared that the $21,000,000 owing to the banks was to be protected with securities; and with considerable finesse, which he is gradually assuming, he proceeded to demand of my honoured leader, after declaring that they had thrown on the table every atom of information in regard to the matter, what he would say as to where this money was
to be found that was to pay the people to whom the Canadian Northern railway was indebted. Then my hon. friend drifted away from the subject and you will not find, from one end of his speech to the other, the information which for the first time we have been able to abstract from him to-day, as to how the men who aTe owed the $21,000,000 are to get their money. My hon. friend the other night, extolled to the House the virtues and the advantages and the glory of the Canadian Northern railway. Why, he said, we advance the money, the whole $45,000,000, upon the guarantee of the Canadian Northern railway and we will be better off than this country was under the arrangement made by the ex-Minister of Railways when an advance was made to the Canadian Northern Ontario railway. He said that if you added the $45,000,000 to the total amount of the bond indebtedness of the Canadian Northern railway you would have an amount which would be less or practically the same as the $35,000 a mile given to the Canadian Northern railway. My hon. friend knew that he was about $8,000 or $10,000 to the mile out.
Oh, no.

My hon. friend will find that the bond issue of the Canadian Northern to-day is $191,933,000 odd. My hon. friend advances the proposition that if you added the $45,000,000 which you are loaning to this company to the $191,000,000 you would only be in the vicinity of $35,000 a mile. If my hon. friend will figure it up, he will find that the cost is about $44,000 a mile.
The figures given by my hon. friend are correct if he includes the equipment bonds. Had the old Government any security on the equipment?

My hon. friend is
dodging the point.
Not at all. Eliminate the security on the lands and the equipment, as it should be eliminated, and it figures out at $35,000 a mile.

My hon. friend, as
usual, is avoiding the point. Instead of coming to Parliament and explaining this agreement, as an associate member of the Government, a rightly constituted minister should do, he goes off into side issues. I have taken his figures from the blue book to show that instead of the road being mortgaged for $35,000 a mile it is

mortgaged for $44,000 or $45,000. He is only out by $9,000 or $10,000 a mile. Then in regard to this mysterious equipment trust. My hon. friend was rather in doubt about this trust from the very beginning. If you turn to the Votes and Proceedings of the 28th April, when this great measure first saw the light, you will find that in the first schedule my hon. friend had included the rolling stock and equipment of any of the companies mentioned therein, and he also included the Manitoba railway (former name: Northern Pacific and Manitoba Railway). After the Prime Minister had explained that somebody, by mistake, had sent a rough draft instead of the final document to the printer, my hon. friend cut out this rolling stock and equipment and since the 30th April it has not appeared in the resolutions. My hon. friend knows that. He also knows that this security for the proposed guarantee does not attach to a single car or locomotive. He also knows that if there is an equipment trust in regard to the railways mentioned in Part 1 of the second schedule, this country gets no security on even an engine or box car in any one of those companies.
No, I do not. We get security on just the same property, as if those words had been left in. We get security on the Canadian Northern rolling stock because we have a floating mortgage.
Since my hon. friend is beginning to explain, perhaps he will tell us why he put those words in, in the first irrstance.

Nothing was in my mind in the first instance because I did not put them in. The Manitoba leased lines were there just by way of indicating that they were to come in as part of the Canadian Northern property. They come in as part of the physical assets of the Canadian Northern, just as does the line between Portage and Winnipeg.
Have you equipment mortgages upon the line?

Certainly, there are
equipment mortgages, and we get security on the equity of the Canadian Northern in them.

My hon. friend knows very well that when the hon. member for Calgary discussed with him yesterday as to what was done with the surplus, he started a discussion on the equipment. Mackenzie

and Mann go to the car men, buy the cars from them and give them their notes, and then sell the cars to the Imperial Rolling Stock Company at a profit.
Oh, no.

Is my hon. friend willing to give a guarantee that they do not make a profit? Why do not the Imperial Equipment Trust go to the implement men in the first place to buy rolling stock like any other great railway?
Every other railway does not.

Excuse me, my information upon that point is quite as accurate as my hon. friend's. I say that the great railroads purchase through their equipment companies from the car people and implement men, and in this respect there is a very great difference between the Canadian Northern and other companies. I disagree with my hon. friend's views on this point. Under the terms of this arrangement, whereby we only get a mortgage on the shares, and where equipment is not specially set out, I submit that we do not get a lien upon a single box car, passenger car, or locomotive in any one of those companies. The Prime Minister told us that one of the things this country was getting was a traffic arrangement with the Canadian Northern railway. Sir William Mackenzie's letter of March 6 is a very astute document. On March 5, he wrote the right hon. Prime Minister saying that it was essential for the reasons mentioned in the memoranda that the Canadian Northern receive further Government aid. Things moved quickly after that. Although on the 3rd of March the Finance Minister knew nothing whatever about the business, Sir William Mackenzie wrote to the right hon. Prime Minister on March 6, as follows:
Dear Sir,-It has been suggested that an agreement should be made between the Canadian Northern railway and the Government in connection with the company's application for assistance, providing for an exchange of traffic between the company's lines of railway and the Intercolonial railway at Quebec. To an arrangement of this kind, the company is agreeable, and it is suggested that the arrangement should be of such nature that the Intercolonial would secure all the benefits, from traffic originating on the company's lines and consigned to points on the Intercolonial railway, that it would have were it the eastern part of the Canadian Northern Railway system. Naturally, the Canadian Northern would expect the same benefits from

traffic originating on the lines of the Intercolonial railway.
I am convinced that an arrangement of this kind is practical and would result in benefit to the two railway systems affected, and if the members of your Government are of the same opinion, I would suggest that provision be made in such legislation as may be passed in connection with the company's application for aid, empowering the interested parties to enter into the necessary agreements.
Tours very truly,
ffm. Mackenzie,
President.
Mark the delightful candour and kindness of the Canadian Northern. They are willing to assent to this traffic arrangement. Sir William Mackenzie and the Canadian Northern have been trying for the last five or six years to get running rights over the Intercolonial. They were hoping to get to Quebec, and the height of their ambition was to' get running Tights over the Intercolonial railway from there down to the sea, and so, on March 6, after Mr. Lash had been mesmerizing the Solicitor General for a little while and had got him into a proper frame of mind, the astute president of the Canadian Northern comes along and says: If you people want me to make an arrangement of this kind, I am agreeable. The Canadian Pacific railway for the last ten years have been trying to get running rights over the Intercolonial railway from St. John to Halifax, but the Government would not consent. Sir William Mackenzie has been wanting this traffic arrangement for years, and now he kindly says: We are going to give all the freight that originates on the Canadian Northern to the Intercolonial. Of course he is. Who else would he give it to? To the Canadian Pacific railway, his rival? Certainly not. He always wa3 going to give it to the Intercolonial railway. He would be delighted to accept the return traffic. He would expect the Intercolonial to give him the return traffic. He was delighted to get it. To get all the traffic of the Intercolonial railway that comes to Quebec handed over to the Canadian Northern railway to go west was a very important achievement for the Canadian Northern Railway Company. They had been endeavouring to get that for years. Graciously waiting for Sir William Mackenzie to accept it is the presentation of the Solicitor General and it is really as good as a play. One of the things that this Government has obtained as a result of this great achievement is that the Canadian Northern railway get an interchange of traffic with the Intercolonial railway. That is really a most interesting phase of this situation. Whatever the country does or does not get in regard to the question of financial terms, there is one thing that Mackenzie and Mann do get out of this agreement and that is running powers over the Intercolonial railway that they had been trying for the last seven or eight years to get and under such conditions that they are obliging the Government to accept the arrangement.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

I was
pointing out the grace and ease with which Sir William Mackenzie responded to the proposition that he should have the running rights over the Intercolonial railway and all other Government railways. Some hon. members who have endeavoured to defend this proposition on behalf of the Government have taken the position that this was a concession in the interests of the country, an offer on the part of the Canadian Northern railway that they would be delighted to carry the traffic that originated on Government railways on the one hand, while the Government railways, more particularly the Intercolonial railway, would be given the opportunity of carrying Canadian Northern railway traffic that might be routed by the shipper. My hon. friend from South Renfrew very pointedly and very ably showed the fact to be that the clause which was put forward by the Prime Minister as being a tangible advantage to Canadian ports and to the Government railways amounted absolutely to nothing, that the clause contained no more, so far as beneficial results were concerned, than was amply provided for under the legislation of 1911. But hon. gentlemen who have been defending this proposition have either chosen to forget or have never seen the delicious irony of the letter of Sir William Mackenzie of the 5th of March. It is really a classic, that document; it deserves to go down to future generations as a specimen of diplomatic negotiations. Its reception is a tribute to the ability of Mr. Lash, who unquestionable penned this document -the solicitor, close adviser and fidus Achates of Sir William Mackenzie. He dealt with the Solicitor General upon whom the whole responsibility of having to do with this measure was placed, the Minister of Finance having absolutely renounced all connection with it-and he put forward the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) to declare that every one was annoyed at the deception practised last winter and the easy way in which he had fallen under the wiles of the Canadian Northern railway. Mr. Lash led the Solicitor General [Mr. Guilbault.3
to believe that the country was getting something especially beneficial; hence we find this covenant in the agreement:
The Government covenants with the Canadian Northern that it will from time to time enter into agreements with the Canadian Northern or with any constituent company, giving running rights over such parts of the Government railways as may be desired and the terms and conditions of every such agreement shall be such as the parties thereto may agree upon, or in default of agreement, as may be settled by the Railway Board.
Now, the Canadian Northern railway, as I have stated, had been for years yearning to get the Atlantic connection for their railway. With all the assiduity and with all the ability-the unquestioned ability- which has characterized their methods in every province of the Dominion, they were able. to get down to the province of Quebec and down to the city of Quebec. But how were they going to get down to the Maritime provinces was a conundrum which they had never been able to solve. And they took advantage of their very necessity for aid, and in order that they might create a complete transcontinental system, to seduce the Solicitor General into giving them absolutely what they had long sought and had been unable to get from any other Government in this country. By these running rights over the Intercolonial railway they will be able to make valuable the property known as the Halifax and South Western. But the Hudson Bay railway from Winnipeg to Hudson bay is also a Government railway. And this company own to Le Pas, as is well known. So this Government is committed to the policy of giving to this company practically the exclusive right of operating over that Hudson bay road ahead of any other transcontinental line. And if the Hudson Bay railway is to be what hon. members from the western provinces have declared it to be, then among the things that have been given up by the country, in addition to entering into partnership with these gentlemen, has been the guarantee to the Canadian Northern railway of practic-a'ly exclusive rights to operate the Hudson Bay railway from Le Pas to the bay. After the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries have spent the huge sums of money that must be spent in rendering Hudson Bay straits navigable and in providing terminals on the bay, the Canadian Northern railway will be given, by virtue of this agreement, running rights over that railway to the bay, the use of the terminals and consequently the

navigation of the bay and straits. So that, instead of an advantage being gained by the Government under this agreement with regard to running rights, as was asserted in the antecedent notice given to the press, these astute gentlemen have befooled the Solicitor General and have obtained from him, in respect of the Intercolonial railway and the Hudson Bay railway, rights which are practically priceless to the country, and which, if Mackenzie and Mann did not secure them under these conditions, they could never obtain under any other circumstances. As I say, this letter, in which Sir William Mackenzie delicately hints that he may be forced to accept this proposition, is the most delicious piece of composition that has ever formed part of any diplomatic correspondence in any communications between contractors and the Government of this or any other country. I am aware that my hon. friend the Solicitor General, who alone, we are told, with many eulogies on his behalf on the part of the Conservative press, conducted these negotiations, had very little knowledge with regard to the Intercolonial railway. Had he consulted the acting Minister of Railways; had the Minister of Finance dealt with this question; indeed, I am free to say that if the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries had had anything to do with the initiation or the carrying on of these negotiations, it would not have been found that that which the Canadian Pacific railway for the last ten years has been unable to obtain upon any terms would be given absolutely for nothing to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. As my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has for many years been endeavouring to obtain running rights from St. John to Halifax, and has been willing to pay for them, but they have been unable to get them. Yet when these gentlemen, whom my friend the hon. member for Calgary has characterized as mendicants, come here and ask this Government to enter into partnership with them and to rescue them from their difficulties, they are able to mislead the Government to such an extent that they succeed in obtaining, in respect of the Intercolonial and Hudson Bay., railways, these advantages upon terms which have never before been dreamed of. This is but another evidence of the lack of shrewdness which characterizes this agreement.
The hon. member for Calgary last nig'it
pointed out very aptly the summary methods by which the Government in 1884 were able, in case of default of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, to obtain absolute control of that system without the application of any such complicated provisions as are to be found in this document. Mr. Lash, the astute solicitor, provides in this agreement 'that if default is had and the country comes to the conclusion that it is not possible for the Canadian Northern to pay the interest upon its bonds and that it must go into the hands of a receiver, there shall be given to them a further lease of life. After the Government has taken the extreme step of entering into possession; after they have assumed all the responsibilities of mortgagee in possession, it is provided that they are bound to account for everything that they do in the interim until Parliament meets, perhaps in the following year, and undertakes to deal with the matter. Supposing default takes place after Parliament rises in June and it becomes necessary for the Government, in order to carry on the operation of the railway, to exercise their powers in respect of default and to enter into possession, the railway may be operated by the Government until Parliament meets in the succeeding winter, when, perchance, the gentlemen who control the Canadian Northern will be in a position to make financial arrangements which will compel the Government once more to restore them to the position of management. In that event, they can, if they are dealing with gentlemen unlike the hon. members for Calgary and Kingston, be able to put through an arrangement with their former partners under which they may resume possession and the Government of this country will be bound to account for every cent of receipts and will have thrown upon them the onus and responsibility for every day's operation from the time they assume possession until the time Parliament undertakes deliberately to declare an absolute foreclosure. The hon. Solicitor General, when he distorted the remarks of my honoured leader in regard to the attitude of the Opposition on this question the other night; when he said that we were perfectly willing to give the Canadian Northern the money without any compensation, entirely ignored the position which was taken by the right hon. gentleman, who, on account of his long experience in Parliament, knows better than anybody in this House the powers and rights which were vested in the Crown in 1884 when the loan was given

to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That power, which could be summarily exorcised under the clause contained in the Act of 1884, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary, should be made a provision of this legislation or of any other agreement made between this company or any other company and the Government under like conditions. The hon. member for South Renfrew pointed out this afternoon conditions which every hon. gentleman on this side of the House and, indeed, every hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, and every man in the country, will contend should be attached to any agreement with this company at the present stage. We are told that we have a mortgage upon so many shares of so many subsidiary companies. We are told that we have mortgages upon other shares which have been mortgaged two or three times over. We are told that we have mortgages upon land companies in respect of which no statement has been laid upon the table of the House to show how many bonds have been issued or in whose possession these bonds are-bonds the right of foreclosure under which may be exercised at any moment to the exclusion of the Government of Canada. What about the other companies in which these gentlemen are interested? This Government has agreed to give to the Intercolonial Railway Company running rights over the Intercolonial. In the province of Nova Scotia we have a railway known as the Inverness Coal and Railway Company, a railway which is controlled and operated by the firm of Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, or the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Why did not the astute Solicitor General insist upon that railway forming part of this security? As a security it is very much better than tile Halifax and Southwestern. Why did he not include in the security to be given the large coal properties in the county of Inverness? Why is it that such companies, for instance, as the Toronto, Niagara and Western and the Toronto, .Niagara and St. Catharines railways, which are owned by Mackenzie and Mann-or by this Canadian Northern system group who are asking for this $45,000,000 and entering into partnership with the Canadian Government; why is it that these properties are not included in the list of securities? The Halifax and Southwestern railway runs from Halifax to Yarmouth, in competition with what is known as the Dominion At-
Ian tic railway. We have a railway running from Port Hawkesbury through the county of Inverness, which, together with large coal properties in that county, is controlled by Mackenzie and Mann, and which are of the utmost value to any railway system offering securities to the Government of Canada under such an agreement as this. I do not find that these properties are taken into security; no attention has been paid to them. As the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) very ably pointed out this afternoon, that which we on this side of the House say, that which the people of the country are saying, that which the two gentlemen who sit behind the Treasury benches said is: Why should not these two gentlemen, Mackenzie and Mann, able as they are, having ideals if you will, ambitious as they may be; why should not they, controlling the Canadian Northern Railway system, when they ask the Dominion of Canada to go into partnership with them, do that which the men who were interested in the Canadian Pacific railway did in the early days, have enough faith in the project to put their resources behind the proposition and to stand by it? When they did that they would have a right to come to the Canadian people and ask for consideration. The Solicitor General did not seem to think that that was a necessary and important factor in regard to this matter. We are told in the Conservative press that this agreement was so cleverly drawn, so ably dealt with, that it was impossible for any other man in the Dominion of Canada than the Solicitor General to fool Mr. Zebulon A. Lash, with the same astuteness. Is there any man on the other side of the House who believes that? I am sure after the eulogy of the hon. member for Centre Toronto upon Mr. Lash, in view of the opinion that every hon. gentleman from Ontario entertains about that gentleman, while it is all very well for the subsidized Conservative press of this country to laud the extreme astuteness of my hon. friend the Solicitor General, all such talk is poppy cock and the practical men of this country know just how far Zebulon A. Lash could deal with the hon. gentleman. My right hon. friend who leads the Government, before the honours and responsibilities of office were thrust upon him, was a man of the very highest ideals. Up and down this land he talked about the control that railways exercised

over the Government of this country. He lamented, in tones of the most lachrymose character, the frightful condition into which Canada was thrust when the Liberal Government, under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, made the arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. He stood for a Government-owned railway ini place of a railway-owned Government, and he rang the changes on that all up and down this land. If ever there was a railway-owned Government in this country, from 1867 down to this time, it is this combination that happens to sit on your right, iwho have gone into partnership with a rauway 'by which there is fastened on this country for all time a mortgage of $312,000,000 to start with, which is going to place upon it another mortgage of $45,000,000 and which owes to-day in the vicinity of $90,000,000 more, which this country will have to pay before it gets through with it. Where is the railway-owned Government to-day? My right hon. friend dilated upon the glories and the advantages and the beauty of Government ownership in this country. Why, if the people are going to pay foT a railway should they not own and operate it? That was the sentiment, that was his promise. Starting from that promise, the right hon. gentleman dilated on the rights of the free people of this country whose money was to be placed behind the enterprise and who were giving this untold amount in order that a few men might sit in control of the rates upon the farmers of the West and upon every other business in the country. That was the burden of his song. Of course my right hon. friend, in the platform which he promulgated previous to 1911, laid down a great many other propositions of that kind. After two and one-half years of responsibility he has not even ventured to fulfil a single one of the assurances he gave the Canadian people. After his blunder of last year, after his failure to make the inquiries which ordinary prudence would have demanded when they came asking the sum of $15,000,000, still when these gentlemen came to him in extremis this year, declaring appealingly that this money was essential to them, without giving any reasons, my right hon. friend forgot all he had ever said about a railway-owned Government and a Government-owned railway and capitulated through the Solicitor General to Zebulon A. Lash, one of the eighteen men who had given him support
in the elections of 1911. Why did not the right hon. gentleman, if he believed in all he said about the desirability of a Government-owned railway, apply himself with assiduity to the task, when the opportunity came to him, of obtaining control over this enterprise, and not palter with the situation and give us this talk about putting up $45,000,000 and obtaining $33,000,000 of stock in return, of putting Canada and her credit in partnership with and under the control and dictation of two men in this country? Why did not my right hon. friend, when these people came to him, as his supporter said, as mendicants, be true to himself and fulfil at least one of the promises that he gave to the Canadian people in regard to this whole question of railway management? And yet this House and this country are seriously asked to accept this proposition. There is not an hon. gentleman outside of the Ministry who has spoken on this question, but who has apologized for the bargain. I venture to say that hon. gentlemen who sit behind this Government will not venture to come before the House and the country and declare that this agreement is the best one which the Government could have made under the circumstances. I fear that we have at last in this country reached that stage when, for the Canadian people, for the world in general, at last we have a railroad-owned Government in reality. Had this Government no sense of responsibility after their experience of last year, after the Minister of Finance had been fooled, after the right hon. gentleman the Prime Minister had been misled? If they had learned the lesson which the hon. gentleman from St. Antoine division (Mr. Ames) indicated they should have learned,, why did they not have a full and complete investigation into the affairs of the Canadian Northern railway? Why do they not have it now? It is ail very well, after the Minister of Finance on the 3rd of March declaring that there was nothing doing, after the Prime Minister on the 6th of March, in answer to a question which I placed upon the Order Paper, declaring that if there was any announcement to be made it would be made in due time, it is all very well with this letter of Sir William Mackenzie declaring that $45,000,000 was essential to him, to come to us and tell us that they had sent their auditors from the Railway Department and the Finance Department and had looked over the statements which the company submitted and that the auditors had told them that these

statements were all right, and because they were all right the Government did not propose to take control of this railway but to practically go out and buy some more stock in it. They say: we bought $7,000,000 last year for which we paid over $200. Now we are going to buy $33,000,000 worth and we are getting it cheaper than last year, we are only going to pay $45,000,000 or about $150. Everybody in Canada should take off their hats and thank Heaven that we have a Government of such splendid erudition, such great business capacity, who come forward and say:	It
is true we were fooled last year; it is true we have made no investigation although Parliament insisted that it should be made; but, after all, we ask this House and the country to adopt this agreement. And why? Because some untold evil that nobody suggests the nature of may happen to this country. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) gave the lie to the Finance Minister yesterday who has been asserting all along that this country is wonderfully prosperous, and that Canada had stood up under stress better than any other country in the world. The hon. member for St. Antoine said that financial conditions and the stagnation throughout the country were such that a problem, had been created which called for solution. Practically the position of the Government is this:	Although the Canadian Northern make no representations in any of the documents that have been laid before Parliament that they need this money other than the fact that Sir William Mackenzie says it is ' essential ' that the Canadian Northern railway should have it, although no statement such as the Canadian Pacific railway made in 1884 has been presented,' this railway-owned Government proceeds to do something, and we are asked to fall dowm and worship this agreement. Before we go into a partnership of this kind we should have a full and complete investigation into the financial position of this company. I need not urge upon this House the necessity of that; the arguments that have been made by gentlemen on the other side of the House are ample and sufficient to warrant us on this side asserting the absolute necessity of having that done in the interests of the country. We are asked to commit ourselves absolutely to finance this proposition for all time to come, because that is what it means; and, financing this proposition to permit the gentlemen who are in control of the Canadian Northern to-day to spend the money after we have provided it. We are asked to 
give them this money on no further information than is contained in the pages of this little blue book. We are asked to assume that times are hard on the other side, and that these gentlemen are in financial difficulties. Although they do not say so in this report we are told that they cannot pay the $21,000,000 that they owe, and that this moment nobody can say, after having heard the Solicitor General deal with this question, whether their creditors are going to get the money or not. Parliament is supposed to give them $45,000,000 under this peculiar agreement. We on this side of the House want to see this transcontinental Tailway protected. We have as much faith, perhaps more, than hon. gentlemen on the other side. I recall the occasion just ten years ago when the proposition was made by my right hon. leader that we should build a second transcontinental railway in Canada, and how the gentlemen who happen to be in power to-day, then sitting-on your left, Mr. Speaker, went up and down this land declaring that it was a totally unnecessary and frightfully extravagant proposition; and hon. gentlemen who came to Parliament in 1904 will recall that they had to fight their way here against hon. gentlemen of the party opposite, who declared that their future and that of their children was being mortgaged for all time to come for a totally unnecessary proposition in this country. Not only do we on this side of the House believe in Canada, but we believe in a third transcontinental as well. We have faith that in the days to come the men and women not only of the western plains, but of all the provinces of our fair Dominion, will produce conditions under which this giant of the north will march forward with more rapid strides than did the country to the south of us. Our great leader twenty years ago told us that the twentieth century was Canada's, and every one of us on this side of the House believe that it will be so. But in order to obtain a third transcontinental, we do not propose to take any gambling chance such as is being submitted to the country at this time. We on this side of the House do not believe that Canada should be saddled with the consequences of this agreement, and that belief is shared by men of promise and ability on the other side of the House. We are proud to know that upon this question the hon. member for Calgary and the hon. member for Kingston, to whom I referred at the inception of my remarks-men whom we on this

side of the House have always respected for their high ideals and true Canadian-ism, although we differ on certain questions of politics-have gone so far as to leave their party, and to declare that this Government shall not have their confidence when they come before this House with such a proposition. Not only that, but last night the Evening Telegram, of Toronto, that citadel of Toryism, gave this note of warning to the gentlemen who sit opposite. Referring particularly to the remarks of the hon. member for Kingston, the Telegram says:
A clear-eyed cynic wrote the foregoing words into the terms of his tribute to a House of Commons other than the assemblage addressed by W. F. Nickle, M.P., yesterday. 'He made rather a spectacle of himself,' was the reward Mr. Nickle earned from a Conservative visitor who does not share the ideals, admire the policies, or serve the interests of the Clan Mackenzie. God help Canada if the old men who should see visions and the young men who should dream dreams are to forever glorify cowardice and despise courage.
Ontario, including Toronto, seems to he represented at Ottawa by seventy-two rubber stamps in the hands of Right Hon. R. L. Borden, whose Government seems to be a rubber stamp in the hands of Sir William Mackenzie. The Canadian Northern Railway bungle and the Grand Trunk Pacific bungle must be straightened Out by heads and hands that had no leading part in the making of these bungles. The situation of the Borden Government is inexpressibly disappointing to Canadians who rejoiced in the results that armed Right Hon. R. I,. Borden with the power of Ontario's progressive enthusiasm. The disappointment of progressive Canadians is aggravated by the spectacle that Ontario Conservatism made of itself in its passive approval of Sir William Mackenzie's attempt to bludgeon and bulldoze the Parliament of Canada.
That is what the Evening Telegram, one of the old-fashioned Conservative pauers in the city of Toronto, says.
Oh, oh.

Since when was John Ross Robertson read out of the party? I listened this afternoon with some amazement to the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Carrick) reading out of the Conservative party the doughty member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett), who, from the Maritime provinces, went into western Canada and carried aloft the banner of Conservatism in the dark days when it was not fashionable to be a Conservative out there. He and the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), who glories in the fact that he learned his politics at the knee of Sir John A. Macdonald, were read out of the Conservative party because they would
not bow the knee to this agreement. And now, forsooth, John Ross Robertson is to be read out of the party because he chooses to believe that the hon. member for Kingston and the hon. member for Calgary have a right to speak their minds in this House. The appreciation of the enormity of this proposition that is put before the Canadian people by this Government will grow as the days go by. This Government attempted to gag public opinion by sending broadcast through the country a false and distorted statement as to the terms of this agreement, before the document was laid on the table of the House. We were told that a most satisfactory, splendid, beneficial agreement in the interests of the Canadian people had been arranged by the astute Solicitor General. The hon. member for Kingston has led the way in pointing out the enormities of this proposition, and I say that the people of Canada will at last learn that we have a railway-owned Government in this country-a Government that, forsooth, was always to stand for the rights of the people, and that was always going to provide for a Government-owned railway. This proposition is one which the Canadian people will not ratify, will not stand for, and we on this side of the House, feeling that we want to put our views at the inception of the discussion upon record in regard to it, I desire, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the Hon. Mr. Murphy, to move:
That the Speaker do not now leave the Chair, but that this resolution be considered six months hence.
Mr. E. W. NESBITT (North Oxfordl: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the resolution and the amendment, I am not going to refer at any great length to the gentlemen who are the proprietors of the Canadian Northern railway and of the subsidiary companies that are interested in this resolution. If all we have heard about Mackenzie and Mann is true, they certainly are entitled to a great deal of admiration for the ability they have shown, to say the least. If it is true that they have nearly completed a transcontinental railway with money secured from various governments, both Dominion and provincial, from municipal corporations and by the bonds that they have sold to the various financial markets of the world, it certainly must be regarded as a tribute to their business acumen and financial skill. Not only, according to the statements made here, have they been able to do that, but they have been able to enrich themselves to

certain extent, that he had a certain control over it. But that would be purely imaginary, we should have really no control; and the presence of our representative there would put us, as a country, in a false position.
If the Canadian Northern railway, no matter by whom controlled, is able to carry its enterprise to a success, every one would be willing that they should make well out of it. I am sure no one in this country grudges to the originators of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the immense means that they nearly all control through the success of that road. And if the Mackenzie-Mann people are able to carry their enterprise through to success, I am sure no one in this country will be jealous; of them. But I do not think we ought to enter into partnership with them. My right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has said he would be willing to loan them the money. And he was criticised severely by the Solicitor General for suggesting such a thing. But the Solicitor General was unfair in his criticism; he put words into my right hon. leader's mouth that that gentleman never used. The unfairness of this course showed in all the worse light because the Solicitor General is a young man and because of the high standing of my right hon. friend and leader,-I am sure that when the Solicitor General thinks it over, he will think so himself. I absolutely agree with my leader that we should assist the Canadian Northern railway, but that we should assist them in such a way that, while they are enabled to carry out their project, we also shall maintain our position, so that in case of default at any time we shall have absolute control of everything there is in the road. And the only way to do that is to have the stock put in the hands of the Government, to be forfeited in case of default. And I am one who would like to see the stock very materially reduced.
Now, my right hon. friend referred to clause (b), at page 14 of the agreement with Mackenzie and Mann, and drew attention to the fact that the Dominion Railway Board were given control over the various railways that went to make up the Canadian Northern Railway system, but that there was a clause reading:
Provided always that any agreement respecting interchange of traffic shall be subject to any agreements now existing with any other company or companies.
I noticed that the Solicitor General was rather amused that the right hon. gentleman should think that that or any agree-

ment could hinder the Dominion Railway Board from having absolute control. But I would refer him to the case of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in which the Railway Board had made an order that conflicted with an agreement which the Canadian Northern railway had made with the province of Manitoba at the time that province guaranteed the company's bonds. That appeal came to the Supreme Court, and it was decided in favour of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta on the ground that the order was contrary to the agreement with the province of Manitoba. Without seeing the agreements that have been made by the various governments with the Canadian Northern railway, I am sure that no lawyer, be he ever so capable, could decide whether the Railway Board would have power or not.
Now, as to the agreement proposed, that the Canadian Northern railway should send all freight over the Government railways, that strikes me as a bit ridiculous. No consignee can be bound by any railway as to how he shall consign his freight. The Canadian Northern railway 'would be absolutely helpless. If any of us were shipping a carload of freight over that road and wanted it carried to a certain point, they would have to carry it to that point or not take the freight at all.
Let me say in a word, I have no objection to Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann making some money out of this enterprise if they can, but I agree with the hon. member for South Renfrew that, if these gentlemen have some means, large or small, and if they are in dead earnest over getting this railway built and are satisfied that this $45,000,000 will finish the road, then it is asking no more than is reasonable, no more than any member of this House, I am quite sure, would ask if he were making a loan privately, that they should pledge their property. There is no reason why the Government should not insist on that. On the other hand, there is every reason why the Government should not be a partner in this enterprise. I ask the Government-with all due deference to this learned and grave agreement-before it is too late to consider their position. I am going to vote for the amendment, because I do not think that the agreement proposed by this resolution is at all satisfactory

to the people. While I am absolutely inf earnest in wishing to see this railway built, and while I absolutely agree with my honoured leader that the country, if not today, then to-morrow or next day, will be quite capable of sustaining this additional transcontinental railway, at the same time we should be cautious about the assistance we give. We should drive the best bargain we can. Or, rather, it is not a case of us driving a bargain; it should be a case of our stating our terms and the people who want assistance coming to those terms.
1 am not in favour of the Government's undertaking the finishing of the road. I believe that the Government, in so far as the letting of contracts is concerned, could ido just as well as private individuals in any part of the work that had still to be completed. But if we were to take the work out of the hands of the present proprietors it would be necessary that we should operate the road when it is completed, or get some person else to operate it. If Mackenzie and *Mann have the ability attributed to them by the various speakers during the course of this debate, then I say that if we search the country with any kind of comb we will be unable to find any one more capable of carrying on this work after it is completed than they are. I for one would much rather let Mackenzie and Mann or some private corporation do the work than have the Government operate the road. I have not the slightest faith in government operation of a work of this kind. No one can tell when the Government may change, and even if the Government does not change, the Minister of Railways of any government would have to be born with a heavenly insight into railway management to be able to take charge of the railway and carry on its operation without making mistakes. All the great railway corporations of America-and they are the only ones with which we can compare ours- are managed entirely by men who have risen from the ranks; men who know the business from A to Z. No matter what party is in power, how are they going to ap-. point a Minister of Railways who has the experience necessary to enable him properly to manage a great transcontinental road? Every man sitting behind the Government would be compelled day and night to have positions available on the railway for persons applying for them. Naturally, we would think that the fellows in our constituency who applied for these positions were quite worthy of them; we would be 342
very inhuman if we did not think so. For these reasons I am absolutely opposed to any government system of operation of rail-[DOT]ways. I hope, therefore, that this Government will reconsider these resolutions and put them into such shape as will enable the Government to give the assistance necessary to ensure the completion of this road. I believe there will be traffic for it, and traffic that will make it pay. I believe also that the country will sustain it. I do not look to see a setback in the West for any length of time, nor do I anticipate any setback in the East. I do believe that the Government will be forced, no matter whether they are willing or not, to give the people of the West some of the things that they have asked for and demanded during the last few years, and the sooner it is done the better. I have much more faith in the Canadian Northern Railway Company, so far as their earning powers are concerned, than I have in the Hudson Bay railway, and I have immensely more faith in the Canadian Northern railway, so far as their earning powers are concerned, than I have in the Georgian Bay canal, which 500 and sometimes 1,000 men at a time, coming here in a body, are asking us to build. I believe that the Canadian Northern railway, properly handled after it is finished, will not only earn interest on the securities that are against it but will earn more than sufficient to pay interest on the securities and give a reasonable rate for freight both east and west as well.
Let me refer for a few moments to some comparisons and nasty insinuations that have been thrown out as to the cost of constructing the National Transcontinental railways. Some hon. gentlemen the other night compared the cost of the Canadian Northern-I am not sure that it was not the hon. Solicitor General-after the $45,000,000 goes into it, with the cost of the National Transcontinental. Let us be fair in this discussion; there will be no earthly comparison, after these roads are finished, between the physical conditions of the Canadian Northern and those in respect of the National Transcontinental railway. Why, then, compare their respective cost? The section of the Transcontinental railway built by the Government runs through an inaccessible country and it was very difficult to convey the supplies and the machinery necessary for the building of the road. This line, however, opens up a new country. Let me say also in support of what my hon.



friend the hon. member for South Renfrew and the hon. member for Port Arthur said, that the Canadian Northern opens up a very much better territory after it leaves Port Arthur coming east than does the Canadian Pacific railway. I have been over some sections of that country and I would not be surprised if a sound earning power on that section of the road from Port Arthur to Montreal were established after the road is completed. I believe that the project will be successful enough once it is carried through, but there is a right and a wrong way to carry this project through, and the wrong way is the present proposition. I offer these few remarks for the consideration of the Government before they try to force this Bill through Parliament against the wishes of the members on this side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened very patiently to the speeches of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House upon perhaps one of the most important questions that has engaged our attention this session. I do not propose to talk about millions or about bonds to-night, because these are things outside of my knowledge. I may be allowed to express some little surprise at the position taken by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). He was in this House last year when the legislation authorizing the granting of $15,000,000 to the Canadian Northern railway was before Parliament. And what did the hon. member do? If my memory serves, me rightly, he walked out of the House rather than vote on the question.
The hon. member will, I hope, allow me to say that his memory is in fault.

The hon. gentleman will
not find his name upon the record in connection with that matter. I propose to discuss this resolution to-night from a standpoint different, perhaps, from that which has been taken by any of the previous speakers. I happen.' to be only an ordinary farmer, and I am inclined to ask this question: has this railway ever done anything for us? If it has, then it seems to me that the proposition now before the House is one which is in the interests of Canada generally. If not then I may be taking a wrong position.

This railway company started a number of years ago by building one hundred miles of railway out of Portage la Prairie to the north, practically through a virgin territory. It then commenced to open up the valley of the Saskatchewan river, where the settlers naturally drifted in. The land was somewhat rolling, slightly wooded, and naturally adapted for mixed farming. I made a statement to the House in the Budget debate that the hope of the Northwest was in mixed farming. Settlers naturally followed the building of this line. Homesteads were taken up. Men were able to perform their homestead duties and work upon the railroad, and out of their savings they purchased implements and live stock, and many of these men became the principal agriculturists of the great Northwest. I believe that not only the Dominion but provincial governments have asked the company to continue their building, because it would be in the interests of the farmers of Canada. The people of the Northwest, especially in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, have reaped considerable returns from the building of this road. This was pointed out, I think, admirably to-day by the hon. membeT for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol), who said tnat $15,000,000 had been saved to the farmers of the Northwest. In Alberta they reduced the rates upon live stock and grain 15 per cent, and in Manitoba 7i per cent, and 3 cents per 100-lbs, on their rate to the head of the Great Lakes.
An advantage has also been secured to the people of the Northwest in the competition which was afforded by this railway. We all know what that means. We know what it means in the older portions of our Dominion, and we know what it means to the success of our Northwest territory. The new line which they are building from Edmonton to Vancouver will afford to the farmers of the Northwest great opportunity of sending their -grain and livestock into that province, while the railway will bring back lumber, fish and fruit from [DOT] British Columbia for their use. The Canadian Northern railway last year handled 30 per cent of the grain and 70 per cent of the livestock of the Northwest.
One of the great difficulties in the building of the railroads has been the municipal aid which has been given io them. This is one thing which I think has been overlooked to a great extent in the building of the Canadian Northern railway. Outside of Port Arthur and the Parry

Sound district, where they received in the neighbourhood of $70,000, as far as I know not one single dollar has been given by any municipality in aid of the Canadian Northern railway.
Coming to the Canadian Northern railway in the older parts of Ontario, the hon. member for Calgary last night skipped over from Montreal to Winnipeg very lightly. He seemed to forget that there were hundreds of miles between Montreal and Winnipeg. The great province of Ontario was practically forgotten. This line from Toronto to Ottawa and then east passes through the richest portions of the province of Ontario. It passes through the county that I have the honour of representing, and I may say from my own experience and knowledge, running as it does between the Grand Trunk to the south and the Canadian Pacific railway to the north, it is doing a splendid work for that portion of the province of Ontario. The Canadian Northern railway will run away to the north in the newer portions of the province of Ontario. The land, I understand, is admirably adapted for settlement. It will afford great opportunities for our young men, who instead of having to go to our Northwest or to the country to the south, can go on that land and still remain in the province of Ontario. That land will be admirably adapted for mixed farming. The Dominion Department of Agriculture has been doing splendid work. They have been developing the live-stock interests especially in the Peace River district, in British Columbia, and in other portions of the Dominion. It is here that the Canadian Northern railway will play a considerable part in being able to market the produce of the work which has been done by the Agricultural Department. I wish to draw the attention of the House to the fact that, in the older and more settled portions of Ontario, the Canadian Northern railway has been doing splendid work. We find that where it has perhaps been impossible for them to continue their steam road, they have been building electric lines as feeders to the main line. These are doing splendid work for the farmers of Canada. I believe that the farmers of Canada fully realize this fact, and when the time comes, and this party and this Government need not hesitate to say when it shall come, that the farmers of Canada will rally around the Government and say: You did wisely and 2421
well when you came to the assistance of the Canadian Northern railway.
1 have listened to the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on both sides, and whilst we may have difficulties upon our side, I venture to make this statement, that when the vote comes to be recorded, we will be able to point out that our oppnents too have their difficulties. I listened to the hon-member for Pictou as carefully as I could to-night. I listened to his speech, forcibly given as it was, and I could not help drawing a contrast between his speech and that of his leader. But it seemed to remain for one of the principal lieutenants of the party to propound their policy. What did the right hon. leader of the Opposition say the other night? He said he was in favour of assisting, in some form or other, the Canadian Northern railway. That was repeated by his lieutenant, the hon. member for South Renfrew, and yet the hon. member for Pictou comes and says: We will do that in six months or later if possible. Mr. Speaker, these gentlemen to be honest, if that would be parliamentary, should remember their record of 1903 and 1908 and 1911, when they came to the assistance of this railroad.
Are they going to let this almost transcontinental Toad go down? Are they going to ruin the prosperity of this country by not coming to the assistance of this road? Or, on the other hand, shall we adopt the policy propounded by the right hon. the Prime Minister the other evening? Have we not security for the proposition that we make? Can any hon. gentleman put his finger upon one single thing that we could have done more than we have? We have practically tied up the road in every possible way.. To-day, the people of Canada are looking to this Parliament because they believe that part of the prosperity of Canada depends upon what shall be done in connection with this third transcontinental railway. I do not say that it was absolutely necessary that this road should have been started, but if any one is to blame because the Grand Trunk Pacific came in between, it is hon. gentlemen opposite. We have these roads, and to-day we cannot do without them. They touch so many vital points not only in the older portions of this Dominion, but in the newer territory as well, that it would be suicidal for this Government to allow these roads to go down. I have an abiding faith that the Canadian Northern with all its difficulties, and despite all its trials in the past, will come out all right,

and that it will play a very great part in the carrying of the products of this country in the years that are to come.
