I wish to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General the dismissal of the postmaster at Bridgeport, in the riding of South Cape Breton. I wish to place on ' Hansard ' and before the House the correspondence that took place between the Post Office Department and the postmaster at Bridgeport, Mr. Joseph McMillan, and some other correspondence. On April 9, 1912, the Postmaster General received the following telegram:
Please investigate Joseph McMillan, postmaster, Bridgeport. Official political partisan. If dismissed beg to recommend Daniel Cameron, Bridgeport, to succeed him.
(Sgd) J. W. Maddin.
In reply to that, Mr. Verret, the assistant Deputy Postmaster General, wrote to Mr. Maddin stating that the usual course was to write to Mr. McMillan first, and afterwards to have the matter investigated. On April 11, 1912, the following letter was sent to Mr. Jos. McMillan, postmaster at Bridgeport:
Sir,-I am directed to inform you that it is represented to this department that you have taken a more active part in elections, federal or provincial, than quietly polling your vote since the date of your appointment as postmaster. The Postmaster General desires to know, therefore, what you have to say in reply to the charge in question.
That letter is signed by William Smith, the secretary, I presume, of the Postmaster General. Mr. McMillan answered this letter on April 15, 1912:
To the Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Canada.
Sir,-In reply to your communication, No. 54747, dated April 11, I beg leave to say that I know of no reason why such a charge as stated should be made against me, and I further submit that I have performed my duties as postmaster honestly, faithfully and impartially, and without fear or favour.
Respectfully yours,
(Sgd) J. McMillan.
In answer to that letter, Mr. Hector B. Verret wrote Mr. McMillan on the 23rd of April, 1912, as follows:

Sir,-With reference to the communication addressed to you from this department, under date of 11th instant, in regard to the representations made to the department that you had been guilty of active political partisanship, and to your reply thereto, dated the 15th instant, I beg to say that in view of the statements made in your letter, it is presumed that you will have no objection to sign the solemn declaration herewith enclosed, which should be attested before a Justice of the Peace.
The declaration to which Mr. Verret refers was signed by Mr. McMillan, and reads as follows:
1.	That I was appointed postmaster in the year 1908;
2.	That since my appointment as postmaster, I have taken no active part in federal or provincial elections ; I have not canvassed or taken any voters to the polls, nor have I offered or given any money or liquor, or represented any candidate at any polling division; I have not checked or verified any list of voters outside any polling station; neither did I take part in any committee of organization or address a meeting in favour of any candidate, and I did not interrupt any public speaker during the course of any meeting.
3.	All I did was to quietly cast my vote.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
And I have signed,
(Sd) Joseph McMillan.
Declared before me at Bridgeport, N.S., this 26th day of April, 1912.
(Sgd) Alex. O. McDonald,,
Justice of the Peace in and for the county of Cape Breton, N.S.
The letter that accompanied that affidavit has no bearing on the case, but the following letter was addressed to Mr. McMillan by Mr. Hector Verret in answer to the letter covering the declaration I have read:
Ottawa, April 30, 1912.
Dear Sir,-I am directed to acknowledge receipt of your solemn declaration, denying the charges of political partisanship which have been preferred against you.
You are no doubt aware that this declaration is as binding as any statement made under oath, and in view of the statements made to this department as to your political activity, your declaration seems inexplainable.
Under the circumstances, it becomes necessary to ascertain who is telling the truth, and the department will consequently proceed to make the necessary inquiries towards this end.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) Hector B. Verret, Assistant Deputy Postmaster General.
The department, then, undertakes to ascertain who is telling the truth as between the gentleman who made the charge against McMillan, and McMillan, whose declaration exonerates him, so far as I

can see, from ever having taken any part in politics since the date of his appointment. Then, there is the following letter, dated Ottawa, May 21, 1912:
Acting under authority of an Order in Council dated the 27th November, 1896, copy of which is herewith, X beg to request that you will undertake a judicial inquiry into certain charges which have been made against Mr. Joseph McMillan, postmaster at Bridgeport, Nova Scotia, in the county of South Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, of political partisanship during his incumbency of that office.
Tour allowance will be $15 per diem, in addition to your actual travelling expenses, and $3 per diem for living expenses. It will not be necessary to employ a shorthand writer or copyist. You will hear the witnesses pro and con and base your report on the evidence.
You will please give Mr. Thomas Callant, Inverness, N.S., and the postmaster due notice of the date on which the investigation is to be held.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) L. P. Pelletier.
H. P. Duchemin, Esq., K.C.,
Sydney, N.S.
Mr. Duchemin acknowledged the receipt of that in a letter dated Sydney, May 25, 1912, in which he says that he will give the matter his very early attention. There are a few other letters in connection with this matter which do not have very much bearing on it. It seems that the gentlemen who made the charges against Mr. McMillan of political partisanship were unable to bring forward any evidence to show that he was guilty. Here is a letter dated Ottawa, August 12, 1912. Apparently it should be dated Sydney:
Hon. W. B. Nantel,
Acting Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir:
I am in receipt of your favour of the 18th instant, wherein you ask me to report at the earliest possible moment, the result of the investigation into charges against Mr. Joseph McMillan, postmaster at Bridgeport, N.S.
In reply I beg to state that no evidence has yet been offered me; that about a month ago, I wrote Mr. J. W. Maddin, advising him that this case was in hand, and that I have received no intimation from him that he has any evidence to offer; also, that Mr. J. C. Douglas, M. L.A., of Glace Bay, in answer to my inquiry regarding this case a fortnight ago, stated that he thought it would be better not to go ahead with it at the present time.
The case is still on my list, and as Bridgeport is so near at hand, I am prepared to take it up at any time the local complainants have evidence to submit. It is entirely in their hands.
Trusting that this explanation will be satisfactory, I remain,
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) H. P. Duchemin.
Next, there is a letter from Mr. Hector B. Verret, assistant Deputy Postmaster
General, dated Ottawa, August 17, 1912, as follows:
I beg to ackowledge your letter of the 12th instant, stating that you have not yet taken up the investigation into the charges preferred against the postmaster of Bridgeport, N.S., Mr. Joseph McMillan, owing to the fact that you have not yet been advised by Mr. Maddin as to what evidence he may have to offer in the case.
In regard to this matter I am to say that a petition has been received for the removal of the Bridgeport post office to a more convenient location, and that this phase of the question will be investigated. In the meantime, you will hold your commission to investigate the political charges against this postmaster, in abeyance.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) Hector B. Verret,
Assistant Deputy Postmaster General. H. P. Duchemin, Esq.,
Barrister,
Sydney, N.S.
Apparently, when they found that they could not substantiate any charge against the postmaster of Bridgeport of political partisanship, the Conservative politicians down in that part of the country decided that they might get around it in another way and on August 17, 1912, they sent a memorial to the Post Office Department asking for the removal of the post office from the site it then occupied to another place in the village, which is really a part of the town of Glace Bay. With this object in view they sent to the Postmaster General, or his department, a petition signed by a great many people. I was rather surprised to see certain names on this petition. I am finding fault with the Postmaster General in this particular-and I asked three or four gentlemen whom I did not think would sign any petition of this kind what they did it for and their answer was that they had never signed
10 p.m. it. I find there are the names of ten persons on this petition who do not get their mail in the Bridgeport post office at all and who would have no reason for asking for the removal of the Bridgeport post office from the former to the present location.
What does the petition say?

The petition says:
We, the undersigned residents of Bridgeport in the town of Glace Bay, do humbly petition you to cause the post office at Bridgeport on the South riding in the county of Cape Breton to be changed from its present location to one which will be more convenient to the great majority of the residents of this section.
Is that it all?

Then it gives the prayer of the petition and the signatures. There is a report and it is on this report that I want to say something that perhaps may be offensive to certain gentlemen who are in the Post Office Department. I do not wish to say anything that may hurt their feelings in any way but I do not believe that the gentleman who presumed to make a sketch of the situation of the post office, and a general sketch of the village itself, ever saw the place or, if he did, he must have known that he was making a sketch that was absolutely wrong. I do not charge Mr. W. E. MacLellan with it but I do charge somebody in his department.
Have you the request of the inspector asking him to report?

That is here but I did not read it. The report is as follows:
I enclose a sketch of the district showing the present and proposed sites of the office, the line of the Sydney and Louisburg railway, the line of the Sydney and Glace Bay Electric Tramway, the Bridgeport colliery, etc. The two sites are little more than one-eighth of a mile apart, but it will he seen from the sketch that the present site is not on the main road,-
That is falsehood No. 1.
-but on a side road and out of the way for the miners and the majority of the population. The proposed site is almost directly opposite the railway station-
That is correct.
and in the immediate vicinity of the colliery.
That also is correct.
The office is served from the Electric Tramway which has stopping places near the present site and also near the proposed site. The contract for carrying the mails between the post office and the tramway is, held by the present postmaster, J. McMillan, for which he is paid $40 per annum. In the event of the transfer being authorized, the service would have to be put into the hands of the proposed postmaster, Dan. Cameron.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) W. E. MacLellan,
Post Office Inspector. The Hon. the Postmaster General,
Ottawa
When the papers were brought down, a copy of the sketch which Mr. McLellan said he enclosed in this letter, was not brought down.
What is the date of Mr. McLellan's report ?

The 21st of September, 1912.
I want to point out that the post office, where it was originally, was on the only 
main street in that section of the town. It was on the line of the Sydney and Glace Bay Tramway company; the cars stopped in front of it and always put the mails off there. The present locality is not on the main road; it is now not even on a public road, but on a road used by the Dominion Coal Company. So far as accommodating the people is concerned, the post office where it was, was in the only business section of the town. There are five or six stores in that section of Glace Bay, every one of which circles the post office where Mr. McMillan kept it; tout where it is at present, there is no business carried on except in the railway station across the way of the Sydney and Louisburg Railway Company, which is a steam road.
Then comes a letter, dated September 26, from the hon. Postmaster General to Mr. J. W. Maddin. I want to be fair in the matter, and I do not know that I have any other criticism than this to make of the Postmaster General. In the first place, Mr. Maddin asked for the dismissal of Mr. McMillan on the grounds of political partisanship. The Post Office Department asked Mr. McMillan if he was a partisan and he replied that he was not. Oh, well, said Mr. Verret, of the Post Office Department, either one or the other is not telling the truth. Then Mr. McMillan was asked to make a. declaration; and he did so, declaring that he had never, since the time he was installed as postmaster at Bridgeport, taken any part either directly or indirectly in political matters, and I believe him. He was appointed to that position, not because he was a Liberal-because he did not vote Liberal previous to that, although he may have voted Liberal after that -but on account of being a friend of a certain gentleman in that district and on account of his place of business being in a central locality. I hardly thought there was a man in this country who could sign such a declaration ; but Mr. McMillan having signed it, I believe that he swore to what was absolutely the truth. Then Mr. Verret, an officer of the department, says:	Mr. Maddin said
that you acted in a partisan manner; you have sworn to the contrary; we will investigate the matter, and find out who is telling the truth. That was in the ordinary course of business, but the department although they searched high and low, could not find any evidence against Mr. McMillan to convict him of political partisanship. This is the criticism I have to make of the Department of the Postmaster General, that, those gentlemen having started to secure the dis-

missal of this man on the grounds of political partisanship and having failed in that, as shown by their own letters to the department, the Postmaster General and his department should have shown more caution in accepting the reports that came to them in connection with the second ruse that was being played for the purpose of getting this gentleman out of his position. When this . matter was brought to my attention, I went to the trouble of writing to Mr. McMillan, asking him for a sketch of this particular part of the town. I knew it pretty well myself, but I wanted to have it in case it was ever asked for. I have the sketch now, and there is absolutely no truth in the statement made in the letter of Mr. MeLellan, that this sketch would show that the present site of the post office was better than the last. As a matter of fact, there are false statements contained in that report. I do not say that Mr. MeLellan made the false statements; I do not even say that the gentleman who reported to Mr. MeLellan did so; but they were made somehow. That is evident to any man who knows the town of Glace Bay. The most startling thing is this, that, when I asked for this return, I asked for a report of the gentleman who investigated this matter, namely Mr. H. P. Duchemin of Sydney. I also asked how much the investigation cost. I think I have shown to the House that no investigation was ever held in connection with this matter at all. Yet the Department of the Postmaster General brings down a return showing that the cost of the investigation against the postmaster at Bridgeport was $17.75. This amount is not given in detail, and I am not very much surprised at that. A charge of $17.75 was made by the gentleman who was asked to investigate this matter and who in his own letter said that the matter was not investigated because there was no evidence forthcoming and because he was told by the officer of the department, Mr. Verret, that this matter should be held in abeyance, and because it was held in abeyance, where then comes the charge of $17.75 for making an investigation when no investigation was made?

Scores of
similar cases.

If there are, I take the ground that a most rigid investigation should be held into all these matters; and I think that I am only doing my duty in bringing to the attention of the Postmaster
General, first, that he and his department should have exercised more caution in having this man dismissed on the ground that his post office was in a certain position, when the thing was started first on the ground that he was a political partisan; secondly, that Mir. Duchemin has charged $17.75 for investigating this case which, on his own testimony and on the testimony of letters from the department, is shown never to have been investigated.
It is outrageous that men should be allowed to lose their offices on pretences of this kind. There are many people in my constituency who have lost postmasterships and other offices; but I am making no great complaint about that; if they have taken part in politics. If they are officials of the Government, and take an active part in politics, they should be willing to pay the penalty. The most of those who have been dismissed, with some notable exceptions, about which I am not going to say anything, are satisfied to pay the penalty by losing any little positions they may have had.	.
I think I have put this case plainly and quite mildly before the House. The Postmaster General should investigate this matter of Mr. Duchemin making a charge of $17.75 for work he never did. While I do not pretend to be in a position always to advise the Postmaster General, I would advise him in cases of this kind, which on their faces are suspicious, that he and the officers of his deparment should take care to see that no injustice is done as certainly has been done in this case.

The fact that there was a bill put in and the amount paid, $17.75, is not explained on the file, and I shall be glad to look into it. If there was no investigation, if Mr. Duchemin did not go to Glace Bay, certainly there was no justification for the charge. We must have had an account of some kind. The fact that he wrote to the department letters about it and looked into the matter and obtained information would take him a full day at all events, and the instructions were that he should have $15 a day. This is a small matter, but still my hon., friend has th.e right to know facts, and I will certainly look into it.

This man never got
any summons to appear, never was asked to appear, and did not appear.

My hon. friend has read the instructions given Mr. Duchemin and knows that he was instructed to notify the postmaster if he held an investigation. If the postmaster did not receive a notice, clearly there was no investigation. My hon. friend has gone over a whole file, and I understand that there is no report by Mr. Duchemin that the case was investigated. Now, that the department should have been told that thie postmaster should be dismissed for partisanship and yet no evidence adduced is a fact to be regretted. I myself have written letters which were easy to .understand telling people who made charges, yet who did not come forward and prove them, that their action was unfair.
Locking the door after the horse is stolen.

The hon. gentleman does not understand what I say. When people have made charges of partisanship against officials, yet have not done anything to prove those charges when the time came, I myself have reproached them for it.
You did not bother your head very much about that in my constituency.

I have bothered my head about it wherever it occurred. I do not think it is faiT to the department or to myself to make charges against an official which cannot be sustained. And it looks like striking below the belt besides. Whether done by my political friends or others, I say it is not fair. Whether this is a case of that kind I do not know. From what was read by the hon. member for South Cape Breton, I should infer that these people, when the time came to prove their charges, said that the time was not opportune.
No, there was simply no evidence forthcoming.

At all events, the
letter will appear on 'Hansard/ It may be that the witnesses who could prove the charges were away at the time. But, let it be remembered, this man was not dismissed on account of these charges; the charges not having been sustained, the man was not dismissed on that account. But we find that a largely signed petition was sent to the department, in which it was alleged that the post office was not at the point where it ought to be. I did not act in this

matter, but the action was taken in this case which js invariably taken-it was referred to the post office inspector. Now, officers of the department are not entrusted as a tuIs with the inveetigation of the charges of partisanship. But invariably, or with very few exceptions, allegations about the management of the offices or their location are investigated, not by outsiders, but by officers of the department, and almost always by the post office inspector. In this case requests for the change in the site of the post office was referred to the post office inspector in Halifax, Mr. Maclellan. I will not say anything either in favour of or against Mr. Maclellan; I have not the pleasure of knowing him. But I appeal to hon. members of this House from Nova Scotia, and I think that there is not one but will tell me that Mr. Maclellan is a reliable officer and an honest man. .He was simply asked to report, and no pressure was put upon him. His report practically says that there should be a change in the site of the post office for the reasons he gives.
But his facts are not correct.
My hon. friend says the facts are not given correctly and that the sketch accompanying the letter is not right.
I am not in a position to speak as to the sketch, not having seen it. Mr. Maclellan may have been misled as to the facts by some one in the locality.
But are the facts correct?
No.

If they are not correct the department will have reason to doubt the efficiency of that officer. This I would regret very much, for I have always been told that Mr. Maclellan is an absolutely trustworthy and reliable official. The hon. member for South Cape Breton says that he has no fault to find with Mr. Maclellan, but Mr. Maclellan is responsible.

I take the ground that if he is responsible he should be held responsible for the false report which he has made to the department, and he should be asked to give the Postmaster General a reason for that false report.

I am not going to disagree with that view. Having been informed by a member of this House, who is

familiar with the place in question, that a report made by one of my officers is not correct, I shall certainly send a copy of ' Hansard ' to this officer and ask him for an explanation. If what my hon. friend says is true, we have been deceived by that officer. Mr. Maclellan had no business to write to the department anything which was not true. His report shows that this post office should be changed; if- we have made a mistake, we have made it because of this report made by our inspector.

I suppose you will
reinstate the dismissed official if you find that the report is wrong?

Certainly, if we have been deceived by our officer. The hon. member for South Cape Breton will agree with me when I say that this man was dismissed because the site was changed and for no other reason. If Mr. Maclellan deceived us in sending the document upon which was based the changing of the site; if the statements he made are not true, we shall certainly see that the matter is righted.

The minister is very
angry-at least, he pretends to be very angry-about getting incorrect information, but the fact that these two matters followed one another in direct sequence is a very suspicious circumstance. When my hon. friend attempts to dismiss a postmaster and is unable to do so for one reason, he invariably finds another reason for taking action. I wish to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to a similar case which occurred in my own constituency. He says it is not fair that the people in the country should complain about postmasters and then fail to substantiate their complaints. According to my view of the way the Postmaster General administers his department, it is a foolish waste of energy for persons to make these partisan complaints, because the Postmaster General is so fertile in resources that he will find some way of getting rid of the officer whether there is a complaint or not. The case to which I wish to direct my hon. friend's attention is the dismissal of Charles McPherson, a postmaster at North Riverside in the county of Guysborough. I had a good deal of difficulty in finding out the name of the man who made the complaint against Mr. McPherson ; I suppose that the name McPherson makes my hon. friend a little suspicious because, no doubt, he had in mind the
celebrated case of the McPherson whom he tried to dismiss four years after he had departed this life. If my hon. friend would consult us on this side about these matters it would be better for himself. The hon. member for South .Cape Breton could have told the Postmaster General all the details about the facts in relation to the matter to which he has referred: If the hon. gentleman had taken the trouble to ask me about the case of the late John McPherson of Tracadie Road I would have been able to inform him that Mr. McPherson had been dead four years and the Postmaster General would have escaped the odium of being charged with digging around in a graveyard and attempting to dismiss a man who had long since departed this life. I want, however, to be permitted to point out how this man Charles McPherson happened to be dismissed. The first communication on the subject is a letter from a man by the name of James R. McPherson, written to the Right Hon. R. L. Borden, Prime Minister of Canada. It is as follows:
Honourable Sir,-Charles McPherson, postmaster of this place, was appointed postmaster on the eve of the last election under the Laurier Administration and he is a strong Grit, always was and always will be. And he supported the Liberal councillor on the 4th of November last. Ever since the Conservative Government came into power X have been looking for his dismissal and I want to be appointed postmaster myself. I have been a Conservative all my life and a near neighbour of Mr. Charles McPherson and as yet I have not got much satisfaction concerning his dismissal and my appointment. Enclosed please find last letter from Mr. G. A. R. Rowlings, which speaks for itself.
Mr. Rowliugs w.as the defeated candidate in the constituency in the last election, and resides in the city of Sydney, N.S. (Reading):
Now, Sir, I wish you to look in this matter and see that this Grit is removed from office.
I am, Sir,
your obedient servant,
(Sgd) James R. McPherson.
This man evidently is not afraid to speak up to the Prime Minister of this country. He charges the man who holds the office with being a strong Grit and with having voted at the municipal election for a Liberal candidate. The following letter was written by Mr. Rowlings:
Sydney, N.S., December 13, 1913. Mr. James R. McPherson,
South Intervale,
Guysborough county, N.S.
Dear Sir,-I have had considerable correspondence with the department about the North

Riverside post office, but I regret to say that I have not had any attention as vet, I have asked for an investigation and they have told me that they would like to know what specific acts of partisanship can be proved. Of course I have submitted the fact that the present postmaster got his position on the eve of the last election.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) G. A. R. Rowlings.
This letter does not seem to have been answered by the Prime Minister. It is answered by the Deputy Postmaster General, on January 22, 1914, as follows:
Sir,-It is represented to this department that since your appointment as postmaster at North Riverside, you have taken an, active part in federal, provincial and municipal elections.
I am therefore directed to request that you will be good enough to say whether this is true. If the accusation is not well founded I presume you will have no objection to signing the solemn declaration herewith enclosed which should be attested before a justice of the peace. An early reply is requested.
I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) R. M. Coulter, Deputy Postmaster General. Mr. McPherson had apparently had no difficulty in making the declaration asked for because there had not been an election since the date of his appointment. It happened this office was open about the time of the last general election and there was no postmaster. The office had been opened but no one had been appointed. After the defeat of the late Government, and about a fortnight before the present Government came into power, I was asked to recommend a gentleman for the post office and I recommended Charles McPherson. His place was centrally located, and he was acceptable to the people, both Liberals and Conservatives. Mr. McPherson makes this affidavit:
I,	the undersigned, postmaster at North Riverside, do solemnly declare:
1.	That I was appointed postmaster in the year one thousand nine hundred and eleven.
2.	That since my appointment as postmaster,
I have taken no active part In federal or provincial elections.
I have not canvassed or taken any voters to the poll, nor have I offered or given money or liquor, or represented any candidate at any polling division. I have not checked or verified any list of voters outside any polling station, neither did I take part in any committee or organization or address a meeting in favour of any candidate and I did not interrupt any public speaker during the course of any meeting.
3.	That I have taken no part in the Liberal interest in the municipal election held on the 4th November, 1913.
4.	All I did was to quietly cast my vote. And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true, and knowing

that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
And I have signed,
(Sgd) Charles McPherson,
Postmaster.
Declared before me at Boylston this 27th January, 1914.
(Sgd) William G. Simpson,
A Justice of the Peace, for the county of Guysborough.
This postmaster was able to comply with all the stringent rules of my hon. friend. He swore that since his appointment he had taken no part in federal, provincial or municipal elections, except to quietly poll his vote. But that does not seem to have helped him very much. Then we have a letter written to the department by Mr. Rowlings. There is consternation now in the department because all the props have been knocked from under their feet and there does not seem to be any way of getting this Liberal postmaster out of office. A letter was written from Ottawa on February 5, 1913, to Mr. Rowlings:
Ottawa, Ont., February 5, 1914.
Dear Sir,-This department lately received through the Prime Minister a communication from Mr. James R. McPherson charging the postmaster of North Riverside with political partisanship and also a letter addressed to Mr. McPherson on the subject by you.
The postmaster, I may say, was asked to sign a solemn declaration in connection with the charge, and he has returned the declaration duly signed. A copy of the declaration is enclosed herewith for your information and for any observations which you may care to make in the matter.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) Hector B. Verret,
.	Assistant Deputy Postmaster General.
G. A, R. Rowlings, Esq.,
Sydney, N.S.
To this, Mr. Rowlings makes this reply:
Sydney, N.S., March 3, 1914. Hector P. Verret, Esq.,
Assistant Deputy Postmaster General, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-Referring to your favou; of February 5, I beg to say that I would recommend that the application of Mr. James R. McPherson for the appointment of postmaster at North Riverside, Guysborough county, he granted. The establishment of this post office was made after the defeat of the late Administration and the present officials appointed several days after the late Government was defeated at the polls There is little doubt that the present official, Mr Charles McPherson, received the appointment as a reward for political services, and I hardly see how the present Administration can endorse his appointment and ratify the same under the circumstances mentioned.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) G. A. R. Rowlings.

You will see that he shifts his ground now and tries to find some other reason that will satisfy the Postmaster General for dismissing this man. He makes no reference to the affidavit, but knowing that there is always some way of getting Liberals out, either by changing the site of the post office or otherwise, he thinks of this device and presents it to my hon. friend. Then we have the order to dismiss Charles McPherson. There is a letter of protest, however, from William A. McDonald, who describes himself as a staunch Conservative. Mr. McDonald says:
North Riverside, March 27, 1914. The Post Office Inspector,
Halifax.
Dear Sir,-I am taking the liberty of writing you a few lines concerning our post office here at North Riverside, which was established about two years ago, it being one of the acts of John Sinclair when the Liberals were going out of power. This office is situated about midway between Boylston and Intervale, about three and a-half miles from each. The present postmaster is Charley McPherson, who had been a Liberal in politics. I may say of him he has kept the office in an honest and trustworthy manner, it has been a benefit to us. Now, a word about myself.
I am a staunch Conservative, and was appointed a delegate by the Conservatives of this polling district, and the Conservatives of this community have asked me to speak in our defence.
There is a man by the name of James McPherson agitating for to get this office for nearly two years. He reports now that he will have it first of April. Now, I will reluctantly have to tell you the truth. The office is in a central place, convenient to the people, held by a Liberal, and Liberals at both sides of it for some distance.
The Conservatives are in the west corner, and just at present we are satisfied where it is, as we sometimes get more flies with honey than vinegar.
In the meantime, if any good honest Conservative will take the office we are satisfied.
I am going to send you a list of property owners so you may know if you receive the right names.
David O'Connor, Thomas Gillie, James Clarey, William A. McDonald, James A. McDonald, John McDonald, Angus McDonald, William McPherson, Edmond McDonald-all Conservatives.
James Fraser, Charles McPherson, Thadeus Leet, Alex. Delroy, Joseph Delroy, C. Bryner, Cris. McDonald, William Cleary, William McPherson-Liberals.
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) William A. McDonald.
It appears the Mr. McDonald's appeal had no effect on the Postmaster General. The facts that this office was in a central place and convenient to the public and that there was no Conservative in the centre of the district who could take this office, seemed to have no influence at all with the Postmaster General.
I have cited this case to show the methods applied by the Postmaster General in getting rid of Liberal postmasters. There was no pretence of any complaint against this man. He was satisfactory not only to the Liberals of the district but to most of the Conservatives- as well. The office was in a central place and everything was going along first rate until this man, James McPherson, cropped up who says that he has been a Conservative all his life and wants the job. There is no evidence that a single person wanted that man removed from office, except McPherson who wanted the job for himself.
What salary is attached to the office?

I have no doubt it is
$35. The salary does not amount to much; the point is the inconvenience that is caused the people of the district by having to go to the west end in order to get their mail, whereas the former office was central. I am only bringing this up as a sample case.
I have a number of other such cases in my desk showing the fertility of resource of the Postmaster General in finding reasons for dismissing Liberal officials who are not guilty of partisanship.

My hon. friend has
explained the facts pretty well, I think, and I do not need to add much to what he has said. I think this office can be regarded as the legitimate patronage of the party coming into power.
Mr. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Kamouraska). -Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take up the question of the dismissals of postmasters in my constituency, as most of them have been relieved of office for various reasons. Let me refer briefly to one case: that of Miss Paradis, of Kamouraska, who was dismissed on account of her political leanings, and also because on the evening of polling day she had put up lights in her window to celebrate the victory of the member for Kamouraska.
Before going any farther and launching into any crilticism of his management of the Post Office Department. I would like to enquire from the Postmaster General whether he will be so kind as to consider an application which I myself submitted, in the course of last summer, for the opening of a post office at a certain point of Kamouraska county called River Menie. That thriving centre is situated on the line of the Transcontinental railway and has a great future in store,, for people are bound to settle

within a few years in numbers at that point where large sawmills are already in existence. I forwarded to the department a petition bearing many signatures. The locality referred to is situated within the limits of the municipality of St. Bruno where the River Menie Pulp Company has a mill.
I fail to see why that petition has not been granted. It seems to me a post office in that locality would be as much in the public interest as the numerous post offices which have been granted to my hon. friend from L'Islet (Mr. Paquet), whom-though I do not see him at his seat just now-I wish to congratulate on the activity he has shown in the matter of the opening of post offices throughout his constituency. I have in hand a report showing that during the year 191213, fourteen new post offices have been opened in the county of L'Islet.
The hon. Postmaster General stated the other day that he managed his department on business lines. However, I do not think the report I have in my hand supports his contention, at any rate as concerns the county of L'Islet. These fourteen post offices bear historic names for the most part. My hon. friend is entitled to our encomiums, the selection of the names bearing testimony to his literary, political and even military tastes. We have, in the first place, Chapais, a beautiful name, well known in the county of Kamouraska. Then we have Rerryer and Artois, the latter I imagine, to satisfy his warlike disposition; Begin, as evidence of his religious faith, La France, Frenette, Ozanam, Deniau, Bourgault, Botrel, the French national bard, Pasteur, the great healer of hydrophobia. However, when 1 reached Pinquet, I was astounded, and also Lachance.
Of course these are beautiful names, but from a business standpoint, I fail to perceive how the department will make a success of it. The total revenue forthcoming from these post offices was $710.81; salaries paid amount to $549.05, and the total expenditure for the carrying of the mails reached $1,093.99. So that the expenditure under all heads made up a total of practically $1,600, while the revenue barely reached $700. As regards some of these post offices, the revenue accruing from the sale of postage stamps reached for a period of two years the fabulous amount of $22. In another office, the revenue from that source did not exceed $19.50, while the carriage of the mails cost $37.50, to which should be added $21.50 for the salary of the postmaster.
I should add that more post offices have been opened since. I am not jealous of the. favours granted to the county of L'Islet, and

I am pointing out the fact solely for the purpose of showing that the department is not managed in a business way and to show how constituencies represented by liberals are dealt with in comparison. Subsequent to the date of that report, the Gia&son post office, among others, has been opened in the parish of St. Aubert. The application was made by my hon. friend from L'Islet, and I cannot do any better than read his letter.
St. Aubert, April 1, 1914. Hon. L. P. Pelletier,
Postmaster General.
Dear Sir,-I recommend the opening of a post office at a point situated one mile and a half to the east of the St. Aubert central post office, at the place of Mr. Georges Fournier, farmer. There are eight families residing at distances of four miles and four miles and three-quarters from the church and central office. On account of the peculiar way in which the settlement is laid out, the new post office cannot be located any further from the central office.
Close to Mr. Fournier's place there is a settlement of labourers, without means of conveyance. We have a storekeeper, a school, a real estate man, a flour mill and fifteen labourers living there. That office would be helpful more particularly to the labourers who, in winter time, cannot easily get their mail. I suggest the name of Giasson. I suggest that the service be daily and the contract awarded to Mr. St. Pierre, at 25 cents per trip, $77.50. 1 am sending the names of those who are asking for that new post office. Thanks.
Tours,
Dr. E. Paquet.

Mr. LAPOINTE.-I say that these are not the signatures of these people.
Will the hon. gentleman take note that in one instance the application is signed by Cyrias Dube?
Abondance !

Yes, Abondance Thibault.

(Reading)-
Joseph Fortin, sr., labourer.

I am only reading the names which have been forwarded to the department.
(Reading)-

Does the hon. member contend that I got the signatures of those people?

I contend nothing of the sort; I am simply reading the names supplied to the department.
To that letter the Postmaster General replied on January 10, 1914, stating that he was instructing the inspector to prepare a report on the matter. Forthwith the post office was opened a mile or a mile and a half away from the office already in existence at St. Aubert.
I now find included in the report a letter addressed to the Postmaster General protesting against the decision,, and giving reasons in support. That letter is signed by Mr. Cyrias Dube and eighteen other citizens of St. Aubert. The letter reads as follows:
Quebec, March 17, 1914. To the Hon. Louis Philippe Pelletier, Postmaster General,
Ottawa.
Sir,-I beg to forward to you herewith a petition from twenty ratepayers of St. Aubert, all affected by the opening of the new post office in that parish, below the church, and designated 'Giasson.' The residents in that township never requested the opening if that town-office, which far from accommodating them is a nuisance, and that, for the reasons stated in the petition I am forwarding to you.
I trust you will have the . kindness of duly considering our request and that you will do away with that post office, which is of no use to us and is rather an inconvenience,
I have the honour to be, sir,

Province of Quebec,
Parish of St. Aubert.
The undersigned ratepayers of the parish of St. Aubert beg to submit to the consideration of the honourable Postmaster General the following facts:-
(1)	That they are residents in the district wherein a new post office bearing the name of Giasson has been opened.

(3)	That it is much easier for the residents in that vicinity to receive and deliver their mail at the post office close to the church, as that has always been the case heretofore, their business calling them at frequent intervals to the village.

As will be noticed, nineteen residents have signed that protest. The representative of L'Islet stated in his letter requesting the opening of that post office that there are not more than twenty persons interested, and, out of that number, nineteen have signed a petition requesting that this post office be closed.
I see by the return that this request was immediately forwarded to the hon. member for L'Islet under cover of a departmental letter dated March 24, 1914. To that letter I find the following answer addressed to the department by the member for L'Islet:
To Mr. H. B. Verret,
Assistant Deputy Postmaster General, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of your letter in reference to the opening of the Giasson post office. I shall take the first opportunity of passing at your office.
Tours,
. Dr. E. Paquet.

The return contains nothing further, which goes to show that he is responsible for the opening of that post office, and that he had been begging to get that post office opened. There is no politics in this connection, and the member for L'Islet will admit that, barring one or two exceptions, all these people supported him at the last election and belong to the Conservative party. That post office was opened with the sole object of enabling some one to earn a few dollars as postmaster and in the shape of house rent. And it is known that in a locality such as this where there is no need for it -whatever, the opening of further post offices is rather harmful. As a matter of fact those interested have been refused their mail at the St. Aubert post office, where they go every Sunday to attend at church, and they are obliged to stop at Giasson to get it.
What was the minister's answer to that protest?

The answer was as follows :
Ottawa, March 19, 1914.
Mr. Cyrias Dub#,
St. Aubert, L'Islet Co., Quebec.
Sir,-I am directed to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 17th instant, enclosing a petition in reference to the Giasson post office, in the Parish of St. Aubert, county of L'Islet.
I have the honour, etc.,
A. W. Throop,
Secretary.
Will the hon. gentleman hand me over the papers?

Certainly. I have
found fault with the policy followed^ by the department as regards the opening of further post offices in the county of L'Islet. I have notv to find fault with the opening of a post office-it was not opened on any application from me-in the parish of St. Philippe de Neri, in the county of Kamour-aska. That parish, according to the last census, has a population of about nine hundred souls. I am sure that the hon. gentleman is well posted on the question. Following on the last election, in that parish as well as in all others, it was deemed proper to dismiss the postmaster if he happened to be a Liberal. The postmaster I refer to did not await dismissal, he resigned at once. A Mr. Roy was recommended by Mr. Potvin, my opponent who was defeated at the polls. The majority in the parish were in favour of appointing some one else, a Mr. Lebrun. Mr. Potvin's

nominee was appointed all the same. But a protest was forwarded to the hon. minister. Matters remained at that point until the month of May, 1912, when the provincial elections took place. My hon. friend the Postmaster General remembers no doubt the trip he made in company with the Minister of Railways, to hear complaints and endeavour to create a better feeling. In the parish of St. Philippe de Neri, an ultimatum was delivered to the leader of the Conservative party, intimating, that, unless the post office was removed from Mr. Roy's to Mr. Lebrun's, forty-five Conservatives, to say the least, would abstain from voting. Those who are familiar with that constituency know what that meant. There followed an exchange of messages between Ottawa, Quebec and St. Philippe de Neri, and finally, on the eve of polling day, an official of the Post Office Department arrived from Quebec, and to the utter surprise of all, a new post office was opened at a distance of about four arpents from the other, under the name of St. Philippe de N6ri West. So that, in a parish with a population of nine hundred souls, comprising a small village, of thirty or forty households, as is to be found in all parishes of that size, there are two post offices. East and West, within an area of a few arpents only. I imagined that would last only until after the election; but I must congratulate the hon. gentleman, he was persevering, and both post offices are still in operation.
What- was the effect on the result of the election?

$200. That is another instance of the minister's unbusinesslike management of his department.
Mr. PELLETIER.-In the case of St. Philippe do Neri, there is room for discussion, but this one is perfectly clear. Here is a man who has a contract at the rate of $220. It should be noticed that the rule of the department is to renew these contracts a long time before the date of expiry is at hand. In this instance we have a service which costs $220 and we find a man who is ready to do it for $200. The distance to be covered would even justify a contract for a larger amount, and even $220 was not too much pay, considering the work to be performed. When the former contractor learned that we had made arrangements whereby that work was to be done for $20 less, he wrote to the department offering to carry on the service for $150. At that price the man could not make a living.
Mr. LAPOINTE.-Why did you not call for tenders?

Because tenders are never called for in connection with contracts for $200 or less. The cost of advertising, etc., would not justify such a course. Our rule is always to award the contract whenever we are satisfied that the price asked for is reasonable. In the case referred to by my hon. friend, we renewed the contract at $20 below the price paid the previous year. That is why Mr. Anderson answered that our arrangements were concluded.

Was the contract
signed?

No, but that does not make any difference, provided the head of the branch has committed himself, it is not necessary that the contract be signed, to bind the department; the contract may be signed only a month or two later, it makes no difference. My hon. friend spoke of what we had done at St. Philippe de Neri-
Your patron saint.

Yes, that may explain why I was generous in my dealings with that parish and granted two post offices. There are many localities with no more than 900 souls and where two post offices are in operation.
There are many places with a population of 900 souls and that have only one post office.

If my hon. friend
from Kamouraska has requests to forward for more post offices, it would be a mistake on his part to believe that I would refuse because the county is represented by a Liberal. I would not think myself justified in so doing. My hon. friend from Rouville stated last year that in following that policy I was only doing my duty. That may be, but I would like people to realize that such is the case. There are a good many constituencies in the province of Quebec where we cannot hope to win, because the Liberal majority is so overwhelming, that it seems impossible that we should overcome it. I shall not give out any names; I would rather continue entertaining some hope. Take for instance rural mail delivery. Is it not a fact that this service is being carried on in constituencies strongly supporting the liberal party as well as in others?
Mr. LEMIEUX.-It is no doubt because liberal constituencies are more enlightened.
Mr. LAFORTUNE.-I have been applying for such a route for two years past and as yet have not obtained anything.
Mr. PELLETIER.-The rules laid down by the department should be complied with. Let us take the county of St. Johns and Iberville for instance, that is one of the constituencies in the province of Quebec where rural mail delivery is organized on the widest scale. That service is not managed to subserve party ends, but on a strictly business basis. When I made that statement last year, my hon. friend from Rouville replied that I was only doing my duty. I know it, and that is my policy on every occasion.
My hon. friend from Kamouraska may rest assured that if he shows that more post offices are required in his constituency, the fact of his being the representative of the county will not by any means be in the way of granting his request.
Mr. LAPOINTE.-There are too many in some places, while there is a deficiency of them in others.
Mr. PELLETIER.-That is a matter of opinion. But as regards the question of deficiency, my hon. friend is not the only one to complain. We take into consideration to a certain extent the question of expenditure and probable earnings of the office; but when the opening of a new post office appears to be needful, particularly in a locality where vehicles are wanting and the distance to go over considerable, to reach the nearest post office, we take the view that

the Post Office department exists to cater to the wants of the public, and we are not overweening on the question of the earnings exceeding the expenditure. For example, if it were shown that twelve or fifteen families are cut off from the rest of the world, their small number would not prevent us from coming to their assistance, and I think that is the right conception of the duties incumbent upon me.
Mr. LEMIEUX.-An application has been made by St. Jean Baptiste de Rouville. Number of citizens have signed that application and are willing to comply with the conditions laid down the the department for the establishment of a rural mail delivery route. However, nothing as yet has been done, and I would ask the minister to be so kind as to look into the matter as soon as possible.
Mr. GAUVREAU.-Before the Minister leaves this subject, I would like to ask for some information. Was there a petition forwarded to him on behalf of the residents of the western portion of L'lle Verte, known as Riviere des Vases, for the opening of a post office?
I cannot say offhand.
Mr. Chairman

The hon. member for L'Islet wishes to offer some explanation in reference to the opening of those new post offices in his constituency, and I trust the hon. gentleman will allow him to address the House for a few moments.
Very well, provided the hon. gentleman agrees not to move for the adjournment of the House previous to my being heard.

Certainly, you will
have plenty of time left to address the House.

I see the hon. gentleman from L'Islet is better acquainted with what is going on in the Post Office Department than the minister himself apparently is; why not appoint him deputy minister?
Mr. PAQUET.-I must thank the hon. member for Kamouraska who takes such warm interest in the welfare of the people in the county of L'Islet. If only he interested himself to the same extent in the experimental farm of Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere.
Does the hon. gentleman think that my suggestions would be favourably considered by this Government?

I regret that my hon. friend should have thought fit to speak sneeringly of the names of electors in my constituency. It is not the privilege of many to be known under the name of Lapointe. I must say that I represent a county comprising many new settlements, a thriving region, and I am not backward in requesting the opening of post offices in sufficient numbers. Long enough that county had been negleoted; long enough our friends on the other side had dismissed all applications, however reasonable, submitted by the representative of L'Islet. Since the coming of the Conservatives into power, I found in the hon. Postmaster General, a man who understands what are the needs of the settlers in the county of L'Islet.
Before we reached power, the settlers and farmers of the county of L'Islet, in order to get to a post office, had to travel over distances varying between seven and twelve miles. That was satisfactory to the member for Kamouraska, but as regards farmers and settlers, the story was a different one. I thought the Postmaster General would be able to do something in their behalf, and I congratulate and thank him for having given some relief to that class of sturdy workers. That may be the reason why the member for Kamouraska is so sour on the Postmaster General and the member for L'Islet who both work in their interest.
In cities such as Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa and others, the people a^e not any better than those I represent, notwithstanding which the mail is distributed from house to house. Why should we not have in our rural districts as many post offices as are required to dispense people of the necessity of travelling over distances of ten miles to get their mail, as was the case under the Liberal rule. The county of L'Islet is progressing, and I am ready to discuss that question with the hon. member for Kamouraska; let him come into my county and upbraid the minister for having done his duty towards that fine agricultural class.

If the hon. member
heard what I said, he must know that far from criticising him, I congratulated him on wielding such influence over the Postmaster General, as evidenced by the fact of his obtaining fourteen new post offices with a resulting total deficit of $1,000 per annum.

I stated and I repeat that the county of L'Islet had been shamefully



neglected under the Liberal rule. To-day a work of regeneration is 'being carried on, since we have icome into power. The hon. gentleman has referred to my parish. The non. member for L'Islet is a genial fellow, but he made a sad mistake when he tried to cast ridicule on the names of my fellow citizens. I would not advise him to repeat the experiment in the parish of St. Aubert. When a man puts his name to a petition hut has not the courage to himself sign it with his own name, I say I have a perfect right to wait until the session is over to personally investigate the facts. And if the Giasson post office should be closed, I shall be the first to call on the minister to do it. I am up against a plot engineered by a Liberal who wanted to get both the post office and the mail contract. Through spite, he got that petition signed, and forwarded it under cover to the hon. minister; however, he had not the courage to sign his own name to the petition, only putting his cross thereto, while he duly signed the covering letter. Under the circumstances, it seems I am justified in postponing until after the session is over the settlement of that matter, and finding out whether the Giasson post office should be closed.
I propose following up the work of providing postal facilities throughout the constituency, so as to put our poor settlers on a footing of equality with city people. I wish to work with all my might in the interest of my electors and let them enjoy the advantages of rural mail delivery.

I wish to protest
against the statement made by my hon. friend that I sneered at the names of those Who signed the petition. I did nothing of the sort, and if the hon. gentleman gathered that meaning from my utterances, he is utterly at sea. As regards Cyrias Dubd whom he taunts for not having had the courage of signing his name to the petition, contenting himself with putting his mark, well the Postmaster General will tell him that one is just as good as the other.
Not when a man is able to sign.

But somebody else
writing to the minister in Dube's name, may have signed for him.

Is not that sufficient
reason for me to delay giving the decision which should be taken under the circumstances?

Does the hon. gentleman contend that the names of the nine-

teen persons who are mentioned in that petition are not actually voters of the parish of St. Aubert?

They are voters of St.
Aubert, but I do not know whether these are their signatures; as a matter of fact, I see that Cyrias Dube who signed the letter addressed to the minister, has not signed his name to that petition, but merely put his mark.

I do not think the hon. gentleman should put forward such a contention. So far, I have had only complimentary references to make to him, but now I am bound to find fault with him. The hon. gentleman was advised by the department that a petition had been received bearing a certain number of signatures and asking that the said post office be closed. His reply to that letter was that he would take the matter up and call at the department. How is it that he has not yet been there, and has not secured the requisite information?

Mr. Chairman since we are dealing with the dismissals of postmasters, I may be allowed to enquire from the minister whether he recalls the incident which took place on Tuesday evening when the removal of the Ste. Scholastique postmaster was considered. I complained on that evening of the action taken by the department on the petitions sent in by certain parties, asking for the emoval of Mr. Raymond and recommending as his successor two persons, the present postmaster, Mr. Presseault, and Mr. Sauve, who, by the way, is not related to Mr. Sauve, M.L.A., at Quebec. The minister answered me as follows:
Mr. Pelletier: I will look into that.
Mr. Ethier: There were many persons surprised that these petitions were not on the file. I am certain they are not of a private character.
Mr. Pelletier: I will instruct the officer in charge of the branch to look into it to-morrow.
It is now Friday, and we have not yet had the promised information. That same evening the Postmaster General, basing himself on the precedent and principle laid down by the former Prime Minister, to-day leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), that all letters addressed to the department and marked 1 Personal," should in no case be brought down on an order of the House for a return, declared himself to be in perfect sympathy with the views then expressed. That is actually the principle laid down by the hon. gentleman.
Without the consent of the writer. Occasionally, I have had letters marked 1 Personal,' which I brought down after getting the consent of the party who wrote them.

Well, since Tuesday I
have not yet had an answer to my request for the bringing down of those petitions, which are in the hands of the minister or filed in the department.
Here is a second question. In the return which was handed to me in connection with the removal of Mr. Raymond, I see there is a letter marked ' Personal.' Now, either the minister has been deceived or is trying to deceive others. How explain the inclusion of that letter in the return, if the rule is not to lay before the House a letter marked ' Personal ' ? Even the copy I have in my hands is marked ' Personal.' That letter is dated December 10, 1913. Again I ask, why is it included in the return? I fancy that when it suits the convenience of the department letters are sent down; if not, they are withheld.
This letter was laid before the House on March 6 last and it reads as follows:
Montreal, December 10, 1913.
(Personal)
The Hon. L. P. Pelletier,
Postmaster General, Ottawa.
My Dear Sir,-In answer to your letter of the 3rd instant, I must say that the gentleman I recommend to succeed Mr. Raymond as postmaster at Ste. Scholastique, is Mr. Wilfrid Presseault. I have no doubt that the aforementioned gentleman will make an excellent postmaster.
Please accept, &c.
G.	A. Pauteux.
This Mr. Fauteux is the same who failed in securing his election, because he did not even know how to prepare his nomination papers. Now, I wish to draw the attention of the House to the manner in which the removal was effected of the postmaster of Ste. Scholastique, which is the chief town of the district of Terrebonne. I might explain that removal was effected through the intervention of the hon. member for Terrebonne, and if Mr. Nantel were present, he might be in a position to enlighten us.
In the redistribution of electoral seats which is being effected, it is proposed to annex the whole or part of the county of Two Mountains to that of Laval. Well I accept that proposal, for I am satisfied that I would get along very well with the good people of Laval. But it would have been a much simpler proposition to unite my county with that of Argenteuil, my 243i
natural neighbour. I invite the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) to come and discuss that question in my constituency, and he will be quite nonplussed at the result.
He might take a lesson in the art of securing an election by acclamation.

Now let us come down to business, I mean let us revert to Ste. Scholastique. Is there a rule laid down for Ste. Scholastique and another for Kamour-aska? In this matter as in the matter of banks, is the principle to be laid down that what is fair as regards Ontario is not fair as regards Quebec? But let us stick to the question, that is, the removal of Mr. Raymond, and let us see under what circumstances it was demanded. In 1896, the postmaster of the district town of. Terrebonne was Mr. Antoine Fortier-what I am about to narrate is a matter of history in the county of Two Mountains. Mr. Fortier was revising officer under the Electoral Franchise Act and he had been appointed by Mr. Ohapleau. Mr. Fortier was postmaster, he was also a Conservative leader in the county. In 1896, when the Liberals reached power, he was, in consideration of his advanced years, retained from 1896 to 1898, the year of his demise. After his death, was he replaced by a Liberal? No, Mr. Minister. You are familiar with Quebec, but you are not quite so familiar with the district of Terrebonne, concerning which you might be posted by your colleague, Mr. Nantel, that silent Mr. Nanitel, who is never seen in the House.
In 1898, we appointed notary Forest, a Conservative also, who had always worked against the Liberal party. He kept the position some time, and then resigned to be replaced by his brother-in-law, Vincent Fortier, always in the same family, and also a Conservative. He resigned for reasons, which I do not wish to state here, and the Government appointed his sister, Miss Annie Fortier, to take his place. In 1903, Miss Fortier got married. I recall these facts in order to show to the Postmaster General that the Liberals did not show any spite, as you are showing against the Liberals.
